sentence: Many decisions are thought to arise from the accumulation of noisy evidence until a threshold is reached.
This process continues until the gathered information hits a specific limit or bound.
This mechanism explains how stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence.
These three factors are the key observable parts of how a decision is formed.
Increased noise is predicted to lead to faster decisions and paradoxically higher confidence.
The extra noise pushes the evidence toward the decision bounds more quickly.
Researchers tested this using a sensory manipulation that mimics noise in the visual cortex.
They verified this method using neuronal recordings from macaque brain areas MT/MST.
In humans and monkeys, increased noise led to faster decisions and greater confidence.
These effects occurred while the accuracy of the choices was only minimally impaired.
The results were in agreement with the predictions of the bounded evidence accumulation model.
The size of the observed effects matched what the mathematical model expected.
The model suggests that volatility disperses the decision variable away from its expected path.
This dispersion causes the brain to reach a final choice in less time.
The sensory manipulation added unbiased noise to regions of the brain that select motion.
The macaque recordings confirmed that the visual cortex responded to this added noise.
The increase in confidence was observed across a range of different visual stimuli.
Both species showed similar changes in how they reacted to the noisy signals.
The bacterial enzyme OspI from Shigella flexneri changes a specific part of the human protein UBC13.
This enzyme converts a glutamine residue at site Q100 into a glutamate residue through a process called deamidation.
This chemical change stops UBC13 from working with another protein called TRAF6.
Normally, these two proteins work together to signal the immune system to fight the infection.
When they cannot work together, the body's NF-κB inflammatory response is silenced.
The modification inhibits the interaction between UBC13 and TRAF6 by disrupting their connections.
Even though the overall shape of the protein does not change, it loses its ability to stick to its partner.
It specifically perturbs both the stable native and temporary transient interactions between them.
The change causes UBC13 to form a new intramolecular salt-bridge within itself.
A salt-bridge is an electrical attraction between positive and negative parts of the proteins.
This internal bond competes with the intermolecular salt-bridge needed to bind to TRAF6.
Electrostatic repulsion between the new glutamate and the surface of TRAF6 also prevents binding.
The new negative charge on UBC13 repels the negatively charged surface of its partner.
Like two magnets with the same poles facing each other, the similar negative charges push the proteins away from one another.
This study shows how a post-translational modification can control protein-protein association.
Small chemical changes interfere with how transient complexes briefly touch and bind.
This discovery explains a subtle way that pathogens can hijack human cell signaling.
Working memory emerges from large-scale network interactions in the brain.
This memory allows people to hold and use information for short periods.
It is an emergent property of many brain regions working together.
Brain regions exchange information through the synchronization of rhythmic activity.
These rhythmic waves occur when many brain cells send signals together.
This synchronization allows for coordination across long distances in the brain.
Researchers used tACS to modulate the right frontoparietal network at 6 Hz.
This method uses mild electrical currents to influence brain wave timing.
The right frontoparietal network includes frontal and parietal regions that support memory.
Induced synchronization improved performance when cognitive demands were high.
Participants performed better on difficult tasks requiring them to remember sequences.
The improvement was seen in a 2-back task where people remember items from two steps back.
The effects of stimulation depend on the relative phase and cognitive state.
Researchers used fMRI to track how these factors changed brain activity.
This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow to track active brain areas.
Synchronous tACS increased parietal activity which correlated with behavioral performance.
The parietal region helps the brain process sensory and spatial information.
Increased activity in the right inferior parietal lobe led to faster responses.
The relative phase of stimulation influences information flow within the network.
This flow describes how different brain parts send signals to each other.
Altering phase synchrony shapes how these network interactions occur.
There is a link between brain synchronization and success in a demanding task.
Helping brain regions sync up can improve performance on mental challenges.
This link shows that the beat of brain waves is vital for task success.
The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is essential for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
This brain region helps with navigation, learning, and memory.
Damage to this area causes spatial disorientation.
This makes it hard to find your way home.
It is one of the first regions to show altered activity in Alzheimer’s disease.
Researchers used optogenetic circuit mapping in mice to study two types of excitatory neurons.
These types are low-rheobase (LR) neurons and regular-spiking (RS) neurons.
Optogenetics is a technique that activates neurons using pulses of light.
These two types of neurons have very different physical shapes.
They also have different ways of firing electrical signals.
Spatial information from the anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum is processed by LR cells.
These LR cells are unique to the RSG and not found elsewhere.
Brain areas involved in direction and position communicate with these cells.
These excitable cells are unique among pyramidal cells in this region.
Non-spatial information from the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex is processed by RS cells.
These RS cells focus on different inputs than their LR neighbors.
Standard neurons in this cortex handle different signals.
They are preferentially controlled by sources of mostly non-spatial information.
Parallel processing is enabled by the anatomical organization of axons and dendrites in layer 1.
The physical overlap of these branches allows for specific communication.
Precise overlap exists between apical dendrites and dense thalamic axons.
This structure permits the separation of input streams.
LR neurons can compute the speed of head rotation from head direction inputs.
Specific synaptic dynamics allow the brain to calculate how fast the head turns.
These neurons turn compass-like signals into a gyroscope signal.
This allows for the robust encoding of angular speed.
The discovery of parallel input streams identifies a neuronal subtype that supports spatial orientation.
Stable petal numbers ensure reliable attraction of pollinators to reproductive organs.
Petals are usually required to open the flower and help attract these insects.
Different insects are attracted to flowers of different shapes and colors.
The plant Arabidopsis thaliana consistently produces four petals in its flowers.
This petal count is invariant and does not change with genetic diversity.
This plant is often used in research studies and its petal count does not change even with genetic diversity.
The related species Cardamine hirsuta has a variable petal number.
A single plant can have flowers with zero to four petals.
Unlike Arabidopsis, this related species lacks robustness in its petal count.
Divergence in the floral regulator gene APETALA1 explains this species difference.
This gene, also called AP1, is a major factor in petal evolution.
Mutations in this gene cause petal loss in both species, making it a strong candidate for the difference.
Arabidopsis AP1 confers robustness by masking quantitative trait loci.
These loci, or QTL, are other genes that control petal number.
Introducing the Arabidopsis version of the gene into Cardamine hirsuta converts its petal number from variable to a stable count of four.
The Cardamine version of AP1 fails to complement this masking function.
This difference is caused by regulatory regions rather than protein coding regions.
The Cardamine version of the gene cannot restore a stable count of four petals when tested in the lab.
Cardamine hirsuta maintains variation despite having the potential for four petals.
Natural populations have enough standing genetic variation to produce four-petalled flowers through recombination.
Natural populations of Cardamine hirsuta typically do not have four petals, but they have the genetic potential to do so.
The way digestive organs undergo regeneration in planarians is not well understood.
Planarians are flatworms that can regrow their entire gut after an injury.
Researchers used laser-capture microdissection and RNA-seq to study the Schmidtea mediterranea gut.
Laser-capture microdissection, or LCM, allows scientists to isolate specific tissue regions from the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea.
The study identified 809 intestine-enriched transcripts that previous studies did not find.
These transcripts are genetic messages that are highly active in the gut and were missed by single-cell studies.
The planarian gut transcriptome is similar to the human duodenum, small intestine, and liver.
This similarity includes genes used for metabolism, bile transport, and transporting nutrients like glucose and fats.
Gene expression shows regionalization along the medio-lateral axis of the intestine.
This means different genes are active in the center versus the outer edges, especially among goblet cells.
The factor gli-1 controls the regeneration of goblet cells in the gut.
A second factor called RREB2 is required for the maintenance and survival of these cells after they form.
This intestinal map serves as a resource for studying regeneration and physiology.
The data helps researchers understand how digestive tissues repair themselves after damage and provides insights into cellular processes.
This genetic map helps scientists understand how other animals might better repair digestive damage.
The study generates new insights into cellular processes whose dysregulation underlies human gastrointestinal pathologies.
Mitochondria are essential for cell energy and must remove misfolded proteins to function.
Damaged proteins can cause these powerhouses to fail if they are not removed.
These organelles are the primary source of energy for the cell.
They are also vital for metabolism.
Ongoing damage can lead to organelle dysfunction.
Researchers used Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast with temperature-sensitive proteins to study this process.
These proteins misfold when the temperature is raised from 25°C to 37°C.
This change allows scientists to trigger the damage.
The yeast serves as a model organism for the study.
This method helps observe the cleanup process in real time.
The ubiquitin-proteasome system breaks down these proteins at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
This means the cleanup happens directly on the surface of the mitochondria.
The proteins are degraded without being moved elsewhere.
The proteasome acts as a molecular machine for destruction.
This confirms the location of the quality control pathway.
The ubiquitin ligase enzymes Ubr1 and San1 tag the misfolded proteins for destruction.
These ligases act as markers to identify which proteins the cell should destroy.
They function as components of the mitochondrial machinery.
The tags are molecular signals for the proteasome.
This specific tagging ensures only damaged proteins are removed.
This cleanup requires Hsp70 chaperones from the SSA family and the Hsp40 chaperone Sis1.
Chaperones are helper proteins that recognize and bind to the misshapen targets.
This is the first evidence for chaperone involvement in this pathway.
They position themselves to recognize the misfolded proteins.
These helpers are essential for the degradation process.
The Cdc48 complex and a mitochondrial pool of Ubx2 also help degrade the proteins.
This study reveals a unique pathway using both cytosolic and mitochondrial factors.
MicroRNAs are small molecules that control how genes work in the body.
One specific type called miR-9 is very common in the brain and neurons.
The role of miR-9 in dendritic and synaptic development was previously unknown.
Dendrites are the tree-like branches that help neurons receive signals from others.
Researchers created a transgenic miRNA sponge mouse line to inactivate miR-9.
This sponge mouse allows scientists to turn off the molecule at specific times.
The study found that miR-9 controls dendritic growth and synaptic transmission.
Neurons in the hippocampus had shorter branches when this molecule was blocked.
The downregulation of a transcriptional repressor called REST is essential for growth.
The miR-9 molecule keeps REST levels low so that dendrites can grow properly.
High levels of REST prevent the normal development of these neuronal branches.
By lowering REST, miR-9 ensures that the genes for growth stay active.
Blocking miR-9 also led to weaker electrical signals between the brain cells.
This shows that the molecule is vital for healthy communication in the brain.
The new mouse model helped track these changes in a living system.
This method provides a way to study gene regulation in specific brain regions.
The transcriptional repressor REST is a direct target of the miR-9 molecule.
Increased REST levels are the major cause of reduced dendritic growth in these mice.
The loss of miR-9 reduced the complexity of the dendritic arborization.
This reduction in complexity impairs how neurons connect within the hippocampus.
Disease transmission by insects peaks at intermediate temperatures and declines at extremes.
Mosquitoes are cold-blooded and depend on the temperature of their environment to survive and perform.
Researchers built a mechanistic model for the thermal response of Ross River virus.
This virus is a significant mosquito-borne pathogen found in Australia and the Pacific that infects 2,000 to 9,000 people each year.
The virus causes debilitating symptoms like long-term joint pain and disability.
It is the most common mosquito-borne disease in Australia and has the potential to emerge globally.
Transmission of Ross River virus reaches a peak at a moderate 26.4°C.
This temperature represents the ideal sweet spot for the virus to spread efficiently between mosquitoes and humans.
The spread declines to zero at thermal limits of 17.0°C and 31.5°C.
Biological processes in the mosquito stop the disease from spreading outside this specific range.
The virus is endemic year-round in the tropics but seasonal in temperate areas.
Southern winters in Australia are currently too cold for the virus to spread effectively.
Climate warming will likely increase transmission in temperate areas but decrease tropical spread.
Warming pushes temperate regions closer to the ideal temperature but may push tropical regions past the upper limit.
A nonlinear mechanistic model is more accurate for estimating temperature impacts on transmission.
Simple models are inaccurate because temperature increases can have positive, negligible, or negative effects on biology.
In northern Australia, the temperature remains suitable for transmission throughout the year.
This results in a nationwide seasonal peak in human cases across the country as different regions reach their limits.
Motor cortical beta oscillations have been known for decades.
These brain waves occur at twenty-five to forty cycles per second in the motor system.
However, their exact behavioral correlates remain unresolved in neuroscience.
These waves often emerge when individuals are paying attention or waiting to move.
Researchers studied three macaque monkeys to investigate these brain waves.
They recorded activity from the motor cortex using electrode arrays.
The monkeys were rhesus macaques implanted with microwire electrodes.
These electrodes recorded multi-scale neural activity from the primary motor cortex and dorsal premotor cortex.
The monkeys used neurofeedback to volitionally control their beta power.
After reaching a specific power state, they performed an arm reach to a target.
A reduction in beta power led to faster movement onset times.
In contrast, an increase in power caused slower movement onset times for the arm reach.
During beta oscillations, population neural activity shifts farther from movement.
The collective activity of many neurons moves away from the required movement onset state.
The distance to the movement threshold is greatest during high beta.
This distance explains why it takes longer to start a reach when these waves are present.
This finding establishes a neural basis for slowed movement onset.
These oscillations compromise the readiness of the motor system to initiate new actions.
Beta oscillations are linked to patterns that slow new movements.
The brain favors a low-risk state over immediate movement readiness during these periods.
Some viruses like Marburg and Dengue benefit from the Nrf2 protein.
Nrf2 is a protein that helps cells turn on genes to protect against damage.
Sulforaphane is a natural product found in cruciferous vegetables that activates Nrf2.
This compound is produced in vegetables like broccoli when they are damaged or chewed.
Sulforaphane blocks HIV infection in primary human macrophages but not in T cells.
Macrophages and T cells are both types of immune cells in the human body.
Reducing Nrf2 levels using siRNA boosted HIV infectivity in macrophages.
This depletion also made the Sulforaphane treatment less effective at stopping the virus.
The anti-viral effects of Sulforaphane are specifically mediated through Nrf2 activation.
This confirms the compound works by triggering the cell's own defense system.
Sulforaphane blocks HIV after entry but before formation of 2-LTR circles.
The treatment stops the virus before its genetic material is ready for integration.
Common anti-viral proteins like SAMHD1 or MX2 were not upregulated.
This suggests that Nrf2 uses a different mechanism to fight the virus.
Activating Nrf2 is a novel way to trigger a potent block against HIV.
This discovery highlights new therapeutic alternatives for controlling infection in immune cells.
Aedes-borne arboviruses like dengue and Zika cause increasing illness and death worldwide.
Arboviruses are specific types of viruses that spread to people through mosquito bites.
Researchers compared transmission drivers for these viruses using data from the Dominican Republic.
Transmission drivers are the factors that influence how a disease spreads through a population.
About 75% of dengue cases occurred in people age <20.
In contrast, only 42% of Zika cases occurred in that same young age group.
Reported Zika infections were highly concentrated among females at 73.8% of cases.
This shows a much higher proportion of women affected compared to the dengue outbreak.
Guillain-Barre syndrome or GBS rates were slightly higher in males than in females.
GBS is a rare condition where the immune system attacks the body's own nerves.
Existing dengue immunity had little impact on the rates of Zika infection.
Having had dengue before did not seem to protect people from catching the Zika virus.
Awareness campaigns likely increased health-seeking behavior among women of reproductive age.
Health-seeking behavior refers to the choice to visit a doctor when symptoms appear.
Experts recommend media campaigns and screening for women of reproductive age during outbreaks.
Screening involves testing people for the virus even if they do not feel very sick.
Anabaena filaments develop a pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts under nitrogen deprivation.
These specialized cells are separated by about ten photosynthetic cells.
The study measured fluctuations of the master regulator HetR using fluorescence.
This method allowed researchers to track gene activity at the individual cell level.
HetR expression fluctuations in nearby cells are coupled over two to three cells.
This coupling shows that neighboring cells coordinate their internal gene activity.
Correlations arise from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Cells communicate by swapping molecules instead of just inheriting traits from parents.
Fluctuations under nitrogen-poor conditions build up on those in nitrogen-replete conditions.
Small differences already exist before the cells face a lack of nitrogen.
PatS, SepJ, and HetR auto-regulation determine the distribution of fluctuations.
These factors act as controls to manage how gene signals spread.
Different inhibitors and septal proteins act at different stages of development.
The study noted specificity between proteins like HetN and FraC/FraD.
Cell-cell communication controls noise to ensure correct developmental patterns.
Managing stochasticity prevents cells from choosing the wrong cell fates.
Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings through a process called dual-adaptation.
This coordination happens when the brain receives feedback for different movements alternately.
Researchers used a target-pointing task where they changed the visual feedback of movements.
This change simulated environmental shifts like those caused by wearing optical glasses.
The visual feedback included horizontal offsets that changed based on the target shape.
Participants saw shapes that ranged from spiky to circular during the training.
The team tested how well participants handled novel target shapes without visual feedback.
These catch trials showed if the learned skills transferred to new situations.
A Bayesian learning model called a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters was developed for the study.
This model describes how the brain learns to associate cues with actions.
Participants applied the mapping for the trained shape most similar to the current one.
They did not learn a linear relationship between the shapes and the movements.
The learning rate decreases as the number of training pairs increases.
Learning slows down when the brain must manage many different associations at once.
The Bayesian model provides a possible mechanism for learning multiple mappings simultaneously.
It explains how the brain keeps separate learning processes for different visual cues.
Many countries where neglected tropical diseases are common lack the baseline data needed for planning.
Without this initial data, health officials cannot prove a disease has passed a treatment threshold.
Researchers created a new system called Integrated Threshold Mapping to map four diseases at once.
This ITM system targets lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM tool tells health officials if a disease is common enough for public health interventions.
It focuses on whether a specific treatment limit has been hit rather than exact numbers.
The new mapping system uses WHO-recommended indicators and specific age groups.
This ensures the data collected is consistent with international standards for disease monitoring.
Researchers tested the ITM protocol in Mali and Senegal against standard WHO mapping methodologies.
The test evaluated how well the integrated approach worked compared to doing separate surveys.
The ITM method reached the same conclusions as standard methods for three diseases.
However, it provided more targeted recommendations for treating schistosomiasis in specific sub-districts.
The integrated approach was practical, feasible, and resulted in an overall cost saving.
Combining the surveys led to savings of 31% in Mali and 19% in Senegal.
This new mapping tool could facilitate the implementation of treatment programs in endemic countries.
Making the first step of mapping more affordable helps start broader disease control efforts.
Organ aging is associated with a reduction in the number of stem cells.
These cells live in a specialized environment known as the niche.
This niche provides the necessary support for stem cell maintenance.
As organs age, fewer stem cells remain in these specialized homes.
In Drosophila female germline stem cells, Notch signaling levels increase with age.
This increase in signaling promotes the removal of cells from the niche.
Researchers used the fruit fly ovary as an excellent model to study these changes.
The germline stem cells are often called GSCs for short.
Notch signaling regulates the adhesion of germline stem cells to the niche.
It controls this sticking by altering the expression of E-cadherin.
E-cadherin acts like a glue that holds the GSCs in place.
High levels of Notch signaling reduce this cellular glue.
This reduction makes the cells less competitive for space.
The age-dependent induction of Notch signaling is partially mediated by Sxl.
Sxl is a protein that normally suppresses Notch signaling in these cells.
It is also known as Sex lethal.
The levels of Sxl drop as the flies age.
This drop allows Notch signaling to increase over time.
Notch signaling in the niche cells decreases as the organism ages.
This decrease reduces niche integrity and the ability to keep stem cells.
While signaling goes up in the GSCs, it goes down in the surrounding niche.
This loss of integrity affects the stem cells from the outside.
These findings regarding cell adhesion may be relevant to metastatic cancer.
HIV infection currently cannot be cured but can be controlled using combinations of multiple anti-retroviral drugs.
These drugs work together to stop the virus from making copies of itself.
Because HIV genotypes vary between individual patients, it is difficult to determine which drug combination will provide effective treatment.
A genotype is the specific genetic makeup of the virus in a person.
Existing HIV treatment models are typically based only on sequence data and do not account for the chemical similarity of drugs.
Sequence data refers to the order of genetic building blocks in the virus.
Researchers applied proteochemometric models that combine chemical properties and protein target properties into a single bioactivity model.
This method looks at both the drug structure and the virus proteins simultaneously.
Researchers constructed robust models to predict HIV drug resistance based on 300,000 bioactivity data points.
The study included three major drug classes known as NRTIs, PIs, and NNRTIs.
Proteochemometric models outperform sequence-only models in classifying resistance and predicting changes in drug susceptibility.
Susceptibility describes how sensitive the virus is to a specific medication.
The study identified previously unpublished mutations in HIV that confer drug resistance.
Mutations are permanent changes in the genetic sequence of the virus.
The proteochemometric models achieved an 84% correct resistance prediction rate on the Stanford University HIV resistance database.
This database is a public record used by scientists to track viral changes.
The researchers added an applicability domain to the prediction tool to inform users about the reliability of specific predictions.
The protein clumping factor B helps S. aureus colonize the nose.
It does this by binding to the cornified envelope in the nostrils.
Clumping factor B is a cell wall-anchored protein.
This surface protein allows the bacteria to attach to host tissues.
ClfB is also a major virulence determinant during S. aureus skin infection.
This means the protein helps the bacteria cause disease in skin tissue.
Researchers found this new role for the protein beyond its known function in the nose.
ClfB promotes skin abscess formation by binding to the host protein loricrin.
This interaction increases the bacterial burden within the infected skin site.
Loricrin is a protein found in the protective barrier of the skin.
Loricrin is a critical ligand that the bacteria use to build abscesses.
An abscess is a pocket of infection that forms in the skin.
The bacteria hijack this host ligand to create a robust structure for the infection.
Vaccination with ClfB induces protective humoral and cellular responses.
These immune responses provide protection and reduce the severity of skin infections.
The vaccine triggers the immune system to produce antibodies and T cells.
The vaccine significantly lowers the number of bacteria found in the skin.
This reduction helps the body clear the infection more effectively.
A lower bacterial burden means the infection is less severe for the host.
ClfB is an important antigen for next-generation vaccines targeting SSTI.
SSTI refers to common skin and soft tissue infections caused by bacteria.
Identifying this therapeutic target is a key step for future medical treatments.
Dengue virus causes about 100 million symptomatic infections every year.
This virus is the most common mosquito-borne virus in the world and half of the world’s population is now at risk.
Infection ranges from mild dengue fever to life-threatening dengue hemorrhagic fever.
Dengue fever is called DF and the severe form is DHF.
Researchers used mass spectrometry for metabolomic profiling of patient sera.
This method identifies small molecules in the blood called metabolites to see how they differ between mild and severe cases.
The study found 29 metabolites that differed during the critical phase.
The critical phase occurs five to seven days after fever starts and is when severe symptoms usually appear.
Bile acids were 5 fold higher in DHF and linked to liver injury.
These levels correlated with higher liver enzymes called AST and ALT which are markers of liver damage.
Uric acid was 1.5 fold lower in patients with severe DHF.
Low levels may lead to a decreased capacity for antioxidant defense against cellular stress.
Chenodeoxyglycocholic acid remained 3 times higher during the recovery phase.
This specific bile acid shows that liver impact can last longer even after the initial fever passes.
These findings suggest new therapeutic targets for managing severe dengue.
Understanding the disease pathogenesis helps in finding better medical treatments for patients.
Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases must have their substrate receptor subunits tightly controlled.
This control ensures the cell maintains a balanced variety of these ligase machines.
Unbalanced levels of substrate receptors can lead to the sequestration of core components.
This competition for parts disrupts normal cellular functions.
Misregulation of substrate receptor components in SCF ligases is associated with cancer.
Many other diseases are also linked to these protein-marking errors.
F-box proteins are typically regulated by autocatalytic ubiquitylation and proteasome-mediated degradation.
This process happens when the proteins are part of an intact SCF complex.
Researchers identified a new degradation pathway for the yeast F-box protein Met30.
This pathway acts when Met30 is dissociated from the Skp1 protein.
The new Met30 degradation pathway requires Cdc53/Cul1 but is independent of Skp1.
It uses only specific parts of the usual machine to function.
This pathway is essential for chromosome stability and defense against heavy metal stress.
It specifically helps yeast cells recover from stress caused by cadmium.
The study assigns biological functions to a sub-complex of Cdc53, Rbx1, and Cdc34.
This smaller team of proteins works independently of the Skp1 component.

Stable petal numbers ensure reliable attraction of pollinators and display of reproductive organs.
Petals are usually required to open the flower and help attract these insects.
Different insects are attracted to flowers of different shapes and colors.
The plant Arabidopsis thaliana consistently produces four petals in its flowers.
This petal count is invariant and does not change with genetic diversity.
This plant is often used in research studies.
The related species Cardamine hirsuta has a variable petal number.
A single plant can have flowers with zero to four petals.
Unlike Arabidopsis, this related species lacks robustness in its petal count.
Divergence in the pleiotropic floral regulator gene APETALA1 explains this species difference.
This gene, also called AP1, is a major factor in petal evolution.
Mutations in this gene cause petal loss in both species.
Arabidopsis AP1 confers robustness by masking nine quantitative trait loci.
These loci, or QTL, are other genes that control petal number.
Introducing the Arabidopsis version of the gene into Cardamine hirsuta stabilizes its petal count.
The Cardamine version of AP1 fails to complement this masking function.
This difference is caused by regulatory regions rather than coding regions.
The Cardamine version of the gene cannot restore a stable count of four petals.
Cardamine hirsuta maintains variation despite having the potential for four petals.
Natural populations have enough standing genetic variation to produce four-petalled flowers through recombination.
These populations typically do not have four petals in nature.
The way digestive organs undergo regeneration in planarians is not well understood.
Planarians are flatworms that can regrow their entire gut after an injury.
Researchers used laser-capture microdissection and RNA-seq to study the Schmidtea mediterranea gut.
Laser-capture microdissection, or LCM, allows scientists to isolate specific tissue regions from the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea.
The study identified 809 intestine-enriched transcripts that previous studies did not find.
These transcripts are genetic messages that are highly active in the gut and were missed by single-cell studies.
The planarian gut transcriptome is similar to the human duodenum, small intestine, and liver.
This similarity includes genes used for metabolism, bile transport, and transporting nutrients like glucose and fats.
Gene expression shows regionalization along the medio-lateral axis of the intestine.
This means different genes are active in the center versus the outer edges, especially among goblet cells.
The factor gli-1 controls the regeneration of goblet cells in the gut.
A second factor called RREB2 is required for the maintenance and survival of these cells after they form.
This intestinal map serves as a resource for studying regeneration and physiology.
The data helps researchers understand how digestive tissues repair themselves after damage and provides insights into cellular processes.
This genetic map helps scientists understand how other animals might better repair digestive damage.
The study generates new insights into cellular processes whose dysregulation underlies human gastrointestinal pathologies.
Mitochondria are essential for cell energy and must remove misfolded proteins to function.
Damaged proteins can cause these powerhouses to fail if they are not removed.
These organelles are the primary source of energy for the cell.
They are also vital for metabolism.
Ongoing damage can lead to organelle dysfunction.
Researchers used Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast with temperature-sensitive proteins to study this process.
These proteins misfold when the temperature is raised from 25°C to 37°C.
This change allows scientists to trigger the damage.
The yeast serves as a model organism for the study.
This method helps observe the cleanup process in real time.
The ubiquitin-proteasome system breaks down these proteins at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
This means the cleanup happens directly on the surface of the mitochondria.
The proteins are degraded without being moved elsewhere.
The proteasome acts as a molecular machine for destruction.
This confirms the location of the quality control pathway.
The ubiquitin ligase enzymes Ubr1 and San1 tag the misfolded proteins for destruction.
These ligases act as markers to identify which proteins the cell should destroy.
They function as components of the mitochondrial machinery.
The tags are molecular signals for the proteasome.
This specific tagging ensures only damaged proteins are removed.
This cleanup requires Hsp70 chaperones from the SSA family and the Hsp40 chaperone Sis1.
Chaperones are helper proteins that recognize and bind to the misshapen targets.
This is the first evidence for chaperone involvement in this pathway.
They position themselves to recognize the misfolded proteins.
These helpers are essential for the degradation process.
The Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex and a mitochondrial pool of Ubx2 also help degrade the proteins.
This complex acts as a molecular machine to process the tagged proteins.
The protein Ubx2 was found to have a dedicated group specifically on the mitochondria.
This study reveals a unique pathway that is distinct from the ER-associated degradation pathway.
MicroRNAs are noncoding RNAs that act as posttranscriptional regulators of gene expression.
One specific type called miR-9 is very common in the brain and neurons.
The role of miR-9 in dendritic and synaptic development was previously unknown.
Dendrites are the tree-like branches that help neurons receive signals from others.
Researchers created the first conditional transgenic miRNA sponge mouse line to inactivate miR-9.
This sponge mouse allows scientists to turn off the molecule at specific times.
The study found that miR-9 controls dendritic growth and synaptic transmission.
Neurons in the hippocampus had shorter branches when this molecule was blocked.
The downregulation of a transcriptional repressor called REST is essential for growth.
The miR-9 molecule keeps REST levels low so that dendrites can grow properly.
High levels of REST prevent the normal development of these neuronal branches.
By lowering REST, miR-9 ensures that the genes for growth stay active.
Blocking miR-9 also led to reduced synaptic transmission and reduced excitability.
This shows that the molecule is vital for healthy communication in the brain.
The new mouse model helped track these changes in a living system.
This method provides a way to study gene regulation in specific brain regions.
The transcriptional repressor REST is a direct target of the miR-9 molecule.
Increased REST levels are the major cause of reduced dendritic growth in these mice.
The loss of miR-9 reduced the complexity of the dendritic arborization.
This reduction in complexity impairs how neurons connect within the hippocampus.
Disease transmission by insects peaks at intermediate temperatures and declines at extremes.
Mosquitoes are cold-blooded and depend on the temperature of their environment to survive and perform.
Researchers built a mechanistic model for the thermal response of Ross River virus.
This virus is a significant mosquito-borne pathogen found in Australia and the Pacific that infects 2,000 to 9,000 people each year.
The virus causes debilitating symptoms like long-term joint pain and disability.
It is the most common mosquito-borne disease in Australia and has the potential to emerge globally.
Transmission of Ross River virus reaches a peak at a moderate 26.4°C.
This temperature represents the ideal sweet spot for the virus to spread efficiently between mosquitoes and humans.
The spread declines to zero at thermal limits of 17.0°C and 31.5°C.
Biological processes in the mosquito stop the disease from spreading outside this specific range.
The virus is endemic year-round in the tropics but seasonal in temperate areas.
Southern winters in Australia are currently too cold for the virus to spread effectively.
Climate warming will likely increase transmission in temperate areas where most Australians live.
Warming pushes temperate regions closer to the ideal temperature but may push tropical regions past the upper limit.
A nonlinear mechanistic model is more accurate for estimating temperature impacts on transmission.
Simple models are inaccurate because temperature increases can have positive, negligible, or negative effects on biology.
In northern Australia, the temperature remains suitable for transmission throughout the year.
This results in a nationwide seasonal peak in human cases across the country as different regions reach their limits.
Motor cortical beta oscillations have been known for decades.
These brain waves occur at twenty-five to forty cycles per second in the motor system.
However, their exact behavioral correlates remain unresolved in neuroscience.
These waves often emerge when individuals are paying attention or waiting to move.
Researchers studied three male rhesus macaques to investigate these brain waves.
They recorded activity from the motor cortex using electrode arrays.
The monkeys were implanted with microwire electrodes in specific brain regions.
These electrodes recorded activity from the primary motor cortex and dorsal premotor cortex.
The monkeys used neurofeedback to volitionally control their beta power.
After reaching a specific power state, they performed an arm reach to a target.
A reduction in beta power led to faster movement onset times.
In contrast, an increase in power caused slower movement onset times for the arm reach.
During beta oscillations, population neural activity shifts farther from movement.
The collective activity of many neurons moves away from the required movement onset state.
The distance to the movement threshold is greatest during high beta.
This distance explains why it takes longer to start a reach when these waves are present.
This finding establishes a neural basis for slowed movement onset.
These oscillations compromise the readiness of the motor system to initiate new actions.
Beta oscillations are linked to patterns that slow new movements.
The brain favors a low-risk state over immediate movement readiness during these periods.
Some viruses like Marburg and Dengue benefit from the Nrf2 protein.
Nrf2 is a protein that helps cells turn on genes to protect against damage.
Sulforaphane is a natural product found in cruciferous vegetables that activates Nrf2.
This compound is produced in vegetables like broccoli when they are damaged or chewed.
Sulforaphane blocks HIV infection in primary human macrophages but not in T cells.
Macrophages and T cells are both types of immune cells in the human body.
Reducing Nrf2 levels using siRNA boosted HIV infectivity in macrophages.
This depletion also made the Sulforaphane treatment less effective at stopping the virus.
The anti-viral effects of Sulforaphane are specifically mediated through Nrf2 activation.
This confirms the compound works by triggering the cell's own defense system.
Sulforaphane blocks HIV after entry but before formation of 2-LTR circles.
The treatment stops the virus before its genetic material is ready for integration.
Common anti-viral proteins like SAMHD1 or MX2 were not upregulated.
This suggests that Nrf2 uses a different mechanism to fight the virus.
Activating Nrf2 is a novel way to trigger a potent block against HIV.
This discovery highlights new therapeutic alternatives for controlling infection in immune cells.
Aedes-borne arboviruses like dengue and Zika cause increasing illness and death worldwide.
Arboviruses are specific types of viruses that spread to people through mosquito bites.
Researchers compared transmission drivers for these viruses using data from the Dominican Republic.
Transmission drivers are the factors that influence how a disease spreads through a population.
About 75% of dengue cases occurred in people age <20.
In contrast, only 42% of Zika cases occurred in that same young age group.
Reported Zika infections were highly concentrated among females at 73.8% of cases.
This shows a much higher proportion of women affected compared to the dengue outbreak.
GBS rates were 0.62 per 10,000 in males and 0.57 in females.
GBS is a rare condition where the immune system attacks the body's own nerves.
Existing dengue immunity had little impact on the rates of Zika infection.
Having had dengue before did not seem to protect people from catching the Zika virus.
Health-seeking behavior is the most plausible mechanism for increased reporting among women of reproductive age.
Awareness campaigns likely influenced this choice to visit a doctor when symptoms appear.
Experts recommend media campaigns and screening for women of reproductive age during outbreaks.
Screening involves testing people for the virus even if they do not feel very sick.
Anabaena filaments develop a pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts under nitrogen deprivation.
These specialized cells are separated by about ten photosynthetic cells.
The study used a chromosomally-encoded hetR-gfp fusion to measure fluctuations using fluorescence.
This tracked the transcription factor HetR at the individual cell level.
HetR expression fluctuations in nearby cells are coupled over two to three cells.
This coupling shows that neighboring cells coordinate their internal gene activity.
Correlations arise from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Cells communicate by swapping molecules instead of just inheriting traits from parents.
Fluctuations under nitrogen-poor conditions build up on those in nitrogen-replete conditions.
Small differences already exist before the cells face a lack of nitrogen.
The inhibitor PatS, septal protein SepJ, and HetR auto-regulation determine fluctuation distribution.
These factors act as controls to manage how gene signals spread.
Different inhibitors and septal proteins act at different stages of development.
The study noted specificity between inhibitors PatS and HetN and septal proteins FraC/FraD.
Cell-cell communication controls noise to ensure correct developmental patterns.
Managing stochasticity prevents cells from choosing the wrong cell fates.
Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings through a process called dual-adaptation.
This coordination happens when the brain receives feedback for different movements alternately.
Researchers used a target-pointing task on a graphics tablet to change visual feedback.
Participants could not see their own arm during these environmental shifts.
The visual feedback included horizontal offsets of 75 mm based on target shape.
Participants saw shapes that ranged from spiky to circular during the training.
The team tested how well participants handled novel target shapes without visual feedback.
These catch trials showed if the learned skills transferred to new situations.
A Bayesian learning model called a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters was developed for the study.
This model describes how the brain learns to associate cues with actions.
Participants applied the mapping for the trained shape most similar to the current one.
They did not learn a linear relationship between the shapes and the movements.
The learning rate decreases as the number of training pairs increases.
Learning slows down when the brain must manage many different associations at once.
The Bayesian model provides a possible mechanism for learning multiple mappings simultaneously.
It explains how the brain keeps separate learning processes for different visual cues.
Many countries where neglected tropical diseases are common lack the baseline data needed for planning.
Without this initial data, health officials cannot prove a disease has passed a treatment threshold.
Researchers created a new system called Integrated Threshold Mapping to map four diseases at once.
This ITM system targets lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM tool tells health officials if a disease is common enough for public health interventions.
It focuses on whether a specific treatment limit has been hit rather than exact numbers.
The new mapping system uses WHO-recommended indicators and specific age groups.
This ensures the data collected is consistent with international standards for disease monitoring.
Researchers tested the ITM protocol in one district each in Mali and Senegal against WHO mapping methodologies.
The test evaluated how well the integrated approach worked compared to doing separate surveys.
The ITM method reached the same conclusions as standard methods for three diseases.
However, it provided more targeted recommendations for treating schistosomiasis in specific sub-districts.
The integrated approach was practical, feasible, and resulted in an overall cost saving.
Combining the surveys led to savings of 31% in Mali and 19% in Senegal.
This new mapping tool could facilitate the implementation of treatment programs in endemic countries.
Making the first step of mapping more affordable helps start broader disease control efforts.
Organ aging is associated with a reduction in the number of stem cells.
These cells live in a specialized environment known as the niche.
This niche provides the necessary support for stem cell maintenance.
As organs age, fewer stem cells remain in these specialized homes.
In Drosophila female germline stem cells, Notch signaling levels increase with age.
This increase in signaling promotes the removal of cells from the niche.
Researchers used the fruit fly ovary as an excellent model to study these changes.
The germline stem cells are often called GSCs for short.
Notch signaling regulates the adhesion of germline stem cells to the niche.
It controls this sticking by altering the expression of E-cadherin.
E-cadherin acts like a glue that holds the GSCs in place.
High levels of Notch signaling reduce this E-cadherin glue.
This reduction makes the cells less competitive for space.
The age-dependent induction of Notch signaling is partially mediated by Sxl.
Sxl is a protein that normally suppresses Notch signaling in these cells.
It is also known as Sex lethal.
The levels of Sxl drop as the flies age.
This drop allows Notch signaling to increase over time.
Notch signaling in the niche cells decreases as the organism ages.
This decrease reduces niche integrity and the ability to keep stem cells.
While signaling goes up in the GSCs, it goes down in the surrounding niche.
This loss of integrity affects the stem cells from the outside.
These findings regarding cell adhesion may be relevant to metastatic cancer.
HIV infection currently cannot be cured but can be controlled using combinations of multiple anti-retroviral drugs.
These drugs work together to stop the virus from making copies of itself.
Because HIV genotypes vary between individual patients, it is difficult to determine which drug combination will provide effective treatment.
A genotype is the specific genetic makeup of the virus in a person.
Existing HIV treatment models are typically based only on sequence data and do not account for the chemical similarity of drugs.
Sequence data refers to the order of genetic building blocks in the virus.
Researchers applied proteochemometric models that combine chemical properties and protein target properties into a single bioactivity model.
This method looks at both the drug structure and the virus proteins simultaneously.
Researchers constructed robust models to predict HIV drug resistance based on 300,000 bioactivity data points.
The study included three major drug classes known as NRTIs, PIs, and NNRTIs.
Proteochemometric models outperform sequence-only models in classifying resistance and predicting changes in drug susceptibility.
Susceptibility describes how sensitive the virus is to a specific medication.
The study identified previously unpublished mutations in HIV Reverse Transcriptase and HIV Protease that confer drug resistance.
One such novel mutation identified by the model is known as T216M.
The proteochemometric models achieved an 84% correct resistance prediction rate on the Stanford University HIV resistance database.
This database is a public record used by scientists to track viral changes.
The researchers added an applicability domain to the prediction tool to inform users about the reliability of specific predictions.
The protein clumping factor B helps S. aureus colonize the nose.
It does this by binding to the cornified envelope in the nostrils.
Clumping factor B is a cell wall-anchored protein.
This surface protein allows the bacteria to attach to host tissues.
ClfB is also a major virulence determinant during S. aureus skin infection.
This means the protein helps the bacteria cause disease in skin tissue.
Researchers found this new role for the protein beyond its known function in the nose.
ClfB promotes skin abscess formation by binding to the host protein loricrin.
This interaction increases the bacterial burden within the infected skin site.
Loricrin is a protein found in the protective barrier of the skin.
Loricrin is a critical ligand that the bacteria use to build abscesses.
An abscess is a pocket of infection that forms in the skin.
The bacteria hijack this host ligand to create a robust structure for the infection.
Vaccination with ClfB induces protective humoral and cellular responses.
These immune responses provide protection and reduce the severity of skin infections.
The vaccine triggers the immune system to produce antibodies and T cells.
The vaccine significantly lowers the number of bacteria found in the skin.
This reduction helps the body clear the infection more effectively.
A lower bacterial burden means the infection is less severe for the host.
ClfB is an important antigen for next-generation vaccines targeting SSTI.
SSTI refers to common skin and soft tissue infections caused by bacteria.
Identifying this therapeutic target is a key step for future medical treatments.
Dengue virus causes about 100 million symptomatic infections every year.
This virus is the most common mosquito-borne virus in the world and half of the world’s population is now at risk.
Infection ranges from mild dengue fever to life-threatening dengue hemorrhagic fever.
Dengue fever is called DF and the severe form is DHF.
Researchers used mass spectrometry for metabolomic profiling of adult patient sera.
This method identifies small molecules in the blood called metabolites to see how they differ between mild and severe cases.
The study found 29 metabolites that differed during the critical phase.
The critical phase occurs five to seven days after fever starts and is when severe symptoms usually appear.
Bile acids were 5 fold higher in DHF and linked to liver injury.
These levels correlated with higher liver enzymes called AST and ALT which are markers of liver damage.
Uric acid was 1.5 fold lower in patients with severe DHF.
Low levels may lead to a decreased capacity for antioxidant defense against cellular stress.
Chenodeoxyglycocholic acid remained 3 times higher during the recovery phase.
This specific bile acid shows that liver impact can last longer even after the initial fever passes.
These findings suggest new therapeutic targets for managing severe dengue.
Understanding the disease pathogenesis helps in finding better medical treatments for patients.
Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases must have their substrate receptor subunits tightly controlled.
This control ensures the cell maintains a balanced variety of these ligase machines.
Unbalanced levels of substrate receptors can lead to the sequestration of core components.
This competition for parts disrupts normal cellular functions.
Misregulation of substrate receptor components in SCF ligases is associated with cancer.
Many other diseases are also linked to these protein-marking errors.
F-box proteins are typically regulated by autocatalytic ubiquitylation and proteasome-mediated degradation.
This process happens when the proteins are part of an intact SCF complex.
Researchers identified a new degradation pathway for the yeast F-box protein Met30.
This pathway acts when Met30 is dissociated from the Skp1 protein.
The new Met30 degradation pathway requires Cdc53/Cul1 but is independent of Skp1.
It uses only specific parts of the usual machine to function.
This pathway is essential for chromosome stability and defense against heavy metal stress.
It specifically helps yeast cells recover from stress caused by cadmium.
The study assigns biological functions to a sub-complex of Cdc53, Rbx1, and Cdc34.
This smaller team of proteins works independently of the Skp1 component.
Many decisions arise by gathering noisy evidence until it reaches a threshold or bound.
This process is called bounded evidence accumulation.
In perception, stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence through this evidence accumulation.
Stimulus strength is measured by the signal-to-noise ratio.
Increasing noise leads to faster decisions, lower accuracy, and paradoxically higher confidence.
Noise here means more variability in the momentary evidence used to decide.
The study used a new sensory manipulation that adds unbiased noise to motion-selective areas in the visual cortex.
This was confirmed by recording neurons in macaque brain areas MT and MST.
In humans and monkeys, increasing noise caused faster decisions and higher confidence with little loss in accuracy.
This effect was seen across different stimulus strengths and was statistically significant when data were pooled.
The size of these effects matched predictions from a bounded evidence accumulation model.
This model explains how motion strength and noise affect choice, speed, and confidence.
The enzyme OspI from Shigella flexneri changes glutamine 100 in UBC13 to glutamate.
This chemical change is called deamidation and is specific to one amino acid in UBC13.
This change silences UBC13’s polyubiquitination activity with TRAF6 and blocks the NF-κB inflammatory response.
Polyubiquitination is a process that helps trigger immune signals through TRAF6 and NF-κB.
Deamidation stops UBC13 from binding to the TRAF6 RING domain without changing UBC13’s shape or enzyme function.
Binding to TRAF6 is needed for UBC13 to activate immune signaling.
Deamidation creates a new internal salt-bridge in UBC13 that competes with a key salt-bridge at the UBC13/TRAF6 interface.
Salt-bridges are bonds between charged parts of proteins that help them stick together.
This salt-bridge competition also disrupts transient interactions needed to form the UBC13/TRAF6 complex.
Transient interactions are temporary contacts that help proteins find and bind each other.
The negative charge on E100 repels the negatively charged surface of TRAF6 RING, further blocking transient interactions.
Electrostatic repulsion occurs when like charges push proteins apart.
This post-translational modification weakens transient complexes and stops protein-protein association.
Post-translational modifications are chemical changes made to proteins after they are made.
Working memory depends on coordinated interactions among large-scale brain networks, especially frontal and parietal regions.
These brain areas communicate across long distances to support memory tasks.
Oscillatory synchronization in the theta frequency range helps coordinate neuronal activity during working memory.
Theta waves are brain rhythms between 4 and 8 Hz that organize activity across brain regions.
Direct causal evidence that oscillatory activity shapes brain network dynamics and behavior in humans is limited.
It is unclear how changing brain waves affects human behavior.

The study used transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate oscillations in a right frontoparietal network supporting working memory. tACS is a non-invasive electrical method that applies rhythmic currents to specific brain areas.
Synchronous tACS improved working memory performance during high-demand tasks like the 2-back test.
Synchronizing brain waves with tACS made participants respond faster in difficult memory tasks.
The effects of tACS depend on the relative phase of stimulation and the cognitive state, as shown by fMRI.
Brain scans revealed that timing between stimulation and brain activity changes how networks respond.
Synchronous tACS during a verbal working memory task increased parietal brain activity linked to better performance.
Higher activity in the parietal region correlated with faster responses in the memory task.
The relative phase of frontoparietal tACS influences functional connectivity and information flow within the working memory network.
Synchronous stimulation increased frontal-parietal connections, while desynchronous stimulation changed posterior interactions.
Working memory performance is linked to large-scale brain synchronization across a right frontoparietal network activated by the task.
This shows that brain wave timing across distant regions supports demanding memory tasks.
The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is important for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
The RSG is a brain area involved in different types of behaviors, including those related to space and other functions.
Researchers used optogenetic circuit mapping in mice to study parallel circuits in the superficial RSG.
This method activates neurons with light to measure how different brain areas connect to the RSG.
The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum send spatial information that strongly activates low-rheobase (LR) neurons in the RSG.
LR neurons are a special type of pyramidal cell that respond strongly to these spatial inputs.
Nearby regular-spiking (RS) neurons in the RSG are mainly controlled by claustral and anterior cingulate inputs carrying mostly non-spatial information.
RS neurons are a different type of pyramidal cell that respond to non-spatial signals.
Precise layering of axons and dendrites in layer 1 of the RSG allows separate processing of spatial and non-spatial inputs.
This arrangement lets LR and RS neurons receive different input types without overlap.
Thalamocortical synaptic dynamics let LR neurons compute head rotation speed from head direction inputs that do not encode speed.
The way these inputs weaken over time helps LR neurons turn direction signals into speed signals.
These parallel input streams show that LR neurons are well positioned to support spatial orientation computations in the RSG.
LR neurons combine information about direction and speed to help with spatial orientation.
A stable number of petals helps ensure reliable display of reproductive organs and consistent cues for pollinators.
Petals open the flower and attract pollinators, so their number affects how flowers signal to insects.
Arabidopsis thaliana flowers consistently produce four petals across different genetic types.
This shows that petal number is a robust trait in this species.
In contrast, the related species Cardamine hirsuta shows variation in petal number from zero to four.
This means petal number is not stable in Cardamine hirsuta like it is in Arabidopsis thaliana.
Differences in the floral regulator gene APETALA1 explain why petal number is stable in Arabidopsis but variable in Cardamine hirsuta.
APETALA1 is a key gene controlling petal number robustness between these species.
Arabidopsis thaliana APETALA1 makes petal number stable by hiding the effects of other genes that control petal number in Cardamine hirsuta.
These other genes are called quantitative trait loci and normally cause petal number to vary.
The Cardamine hirsuta version of APETALA1 cannot replace the Arabidopsis version to stabilize petal number.
Differences in gene regulation regions of APETALA1 contribute to this failure.
Cardamine hirsuta keeps variable petal number even though natural genetic variation can produce four-petalled flowers.
This shows that genetic variation alone does not fix petal number in this species.
Proper function and repair of the digestive system are vital to most animals.
The digestive system is essential for animal survival, so its proper function and ability to repair damage are critical.
Understanding digestive system function and repair requires an atlas of gene expression and cell types.
An atlas is a detailed map showing which genes are active in which cell types.
Laser-capture microdissection and RNA sequencing were used to study gene activity in the gut of the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea.
This flatworm can regenerate all organs, including the gut.
Hundreds of genes active in the planarian intestine were found that previous methods had missed.
This shows the method is more sensitive than earlier approaches.
The digestive physiology and cell types of Schmidtea mediterranea are similar to those in humans and other animals.
Many genes and cell types are conserved across species.
Spatial laser-capture microdissection revealed that gene expression varies across regions of the planarian intestine.
This regionalization is especially clear in intestinal goblet cells along the medio-lateral axis.
Two transcription factors, gli-1 and RREB2, control regeneration and maintenance of goblet cells in Schmidtea mediterranea.
Gli-1 regulates goblet cell regrowth, while RREB2 supports their survival.
The planarian intestinal transcriptome and methods provide resources to study gut function, repair, and regeneration.
These tools will support future research on digestive systems across animals.
Mitochondria need quality control to remove misfolded proteins and keep working properly.
Misfolded proteins can damage mitochondria and affect their essential functions.
Quality control pathways for misfolded mitochondrial proteins are not well understood.
While cells remove misfolded proteins in general, how this happens in mitochondria is unclear.
Researchers used temperature-sensitive mitochondrial outer membrane proteins in yeast as models to study quality control.
These proteins unfold at higher temperatures, mimicking damaged proteins on mitochondria.
The damaged proteins sen2-1HAts and sam35-2HAts are broken down at the mitochondrial outer membrane by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
The cell tags these proteins with ubiquitin to mark them for destruction by the proteasome.
The ubiquitin ligase Ubr1 tags sen2-1HAts, while San1 tags sam35-2HAts for degradation.
These enzymes attach ubiquitin to the damaged proteins to signal their removal.
Chaperone proteins from the SSA family and Hsp40 Sis1 are needed to degrade both damaged mitochondrial proteins.
Chaperones help recognize misfolded proteins and assist in their tagging for destruction.
The Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex, Doa1, and the mitochondrial adaptor Ubx2 help remove these damaged proteins from the membrane.
These protein machines extract tagged proteins to deliver them to the proteasome.
This study defines a unique mitochondrial quality control pathway using both cytosolic and mitochondrial factors.
This pathway is different from other cellular quality control systems and works at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
MicroRNAs are small RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription; miR-9 is abundant in the brain.

Posttranscriptional regulation means controlling gene activity after RNA is made from DNA. miR-9’s role in dendritic and synaptic development is not well understood despite its known function in early neurons.
Dendrites and synapses are parts of neurons that connect and communicate with other cells.
Researchers created a transgenic mouse with a miRNA sponge to block miR-9 in specific brain areas and times.
A miRNA sponge is a genetic tool that binds and inactivates miR-9 molecules.
Blocking miR-9 in mice reduced dendritic growth and changed synaptic transmission in living neurons.
Synaptic transmission is the process of sending signals between neurons. miR-9 lowers levels of REST, a protein that represses gene activity, to allow normal dendritic growth.
REST is a transcriptional repressor that blocks genes needed for dendrite development.
Elevated REST protein levels were found in neurons where miR-9 was blocked.
This increase in REST is linked to the observed defects in dendritic growth.
Vector-borne disease transmission peaks at intermediate temperatures and drops at high and low temperatures.
Mosquitoes spread diseases best when it is not too cold or too hot because their survival and reproduction decline outside this range.
We built a mechanistic model to study how temperature affects Ross River virus spread in Australia and the Pacific Islands.
The model uses temperature effects on mosquitoes and the virus to predict transmission patterns.
Ross River virus transmission peaks at 26.4°C and stops below 17.0°C or above 31.5°C.
These temperatures mark the thermal limits where the virus can no longer spread.
The optimal temperature is largely determined by adult mosquito lifespan.
The model predicts year-round virus spread in tropical regions and seasonal spread in temperate areas.
This matches the seasonal peak in human cases seen across Australia.
Temperature suitability varies seasonally, forcing transmission to zero part of the year in temperate zones.
Climate warming will likely increase virus transmission in temperate areas but decrease it in tropical areas near the thermal optimum.
Most Australians live in temperate zones where warming makes conditions better for spread.
In tropical areas, warming may push temperatures above the upper thermal limit for much of the year.
Nonlinear models are needed because small temperature changes can increase or decrease virus spread depending on current temperatures.
The effect of warming varies along the thermal response curve of transmission, causing positive, negligible, or negative impacts on spread.
Motor cortical beta oscillations are brain waves seen in motor cortex, but their behavioral correlates remain unclear.
These oscillations have been reported for decades without a clear link to specific behaviors.
Three macaque monkeys were trained to control their motor cortical beta oscillations using a neurofeedback task before reaching with their arm.
Neurofeedback means the monkeys learned to change their brain waves by watching a cursor linked to beta power.
Monkeys adjusted their beta oscillatory power to target levels before performing arm-reaching movements.
