The Bayesian model assumes people choose the closest learned movement rather than a smooth rule.
Participants needed explicit awareness of the cue's role to learn and applied the mapping of the trained shape most similar to the current one.
The Bayesian learning model predicted that learning slows down as the number of training pairs increases, which the results confirmed.
The Bayesian learning model matches the data and offers a possible mechanism for learning multiple visuomotor mappings simultaneously.
Vertical control and elimination programs targeting specific neglected tropical diseases can reduce infection prevalence and intensity.
Many NTD-endemic countries lack baseline data needed to start or expand control programs.
Baseline data are basic information needed for planning and advocacy.
Because neglected tropical diseases often overlap geographically, integrated mapping can save resources and improve efficiency.
A new integrated mapping protocol called Integrated Threshold Mapping (ITM) was developed for four NTDs: lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM protocol is resource-efficient and determines if disease levels have reached thresholds for public health interventions.
Thresholds indicate when action is needed in a specific area called an implementation unit.
ITM uses WHO-recommended disease indicators and age groups, sampling mostly at the district level except for schistosomiasis, which uses sub-district sampling.
WHO indicators are standard signs and measures for each disease.
The ITM protocol was tested by comparing it to WHO mapping methods in one district each in Mali and Senegal.
ITM agreed with WHO methods on interventions for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and soil-transmitted helminths but gave more targeted recommendations for schistosomiasis.
ITM was practical, feasible, and showed cost savings compared to standard WHO methods.
ITM used fewer vehicles, smaller teams, and took about half the time to implement.
This integrated mapping tool could help start and run needed NTD control programs in endemic countries.
Stem cells naturally reside in specialized environments called niches that support their function.
As organs age, fewer stem cells remain in their supportive niches, but how this happens is not well known.
In fruit flies, Notch signaling increases with age in female germline stem cells, causing them to leave the niche.
Notch signaling is a cell communication pathway that affects cell behavior.
Stem cells with low Notch activity stick better to the niche by having more E-cadherin, a molecule that helps cells attach.
E-cadherin is a protein that strengthens cell-to-cell adhesion.
Increasing Notch signaling in stem cells speeds up their age-related loss from the niche, partly through a protein called Sex lethal.
Sex lethal helps regulate Notch signaling levels in these stem cells.
Blocking Notch signaling in stem cells does not stop their loss with age and does not change BMP signaling, which supports stem cell renewal.
BMP signaling is another pathway that helps stem cells maintain themselves.
Notch activity decreases with age in niche cells that keep stem cells in place, showing Notch controls stem cell retention both inside and outside the stem cells.
Niche cells form the environment that holds stem cells in position.
Notch signaling controls how stem cells stick to their niche as they age, a role also seen in cancer cells where Notch reduces cell adhesion.
HIV infection cannot currently be cured but can be controlled by combination treatment with multiple anti-retroviral drugs.
Different viral genotypes exist for virtually each individual HIV patient, so the best drug combination varies per person.
Viral genotype means the genetic makeup of the virus in a patient.
Computational models using viral genotypic and clinical phenotypic data can predict optimal HIV treatment regimens for individual patients.
Clinical data shows how the virus behaves in the patient.
Current prediction models use only viral genetic sequences and ignore chemical similarities between drugs.
Proteochemometric models combine drug chemical features and viral protein properties to improve resistance predictions.
This approach links how drugs and virus proteins interact to predict drug effectiveness.
The study used a large clinical database with about 300,000 drug-mutant bioactivity data points covering multiple drugs and thousands of HIV mutants.
Bioactivity data measures how well drugs work against different virus variants.
Proteochemometric models predicted drug resistance more accurately than sequence-only models, with errors below 0.5 Log Fold Change.
Log Fold Change measures how much the virus resists a drug compared to normal.
The models confirmed known and found new mutations in HIV Reverse Transcriptase and Protease that cause drug resistance.
When tested on the Stanford HIV resistance database, the models correctly predicted resistance in 84% of cases, better than previous methods at 80%.
These models can accurately predict drug resistance even for new HIV mutants and mixed virus populations.
The models include a reliability measure based on similarity to known virus sequences to inform users about prediction trustworthiness.
Staphylococcus aureus has cell wall-anchored proteins that help it stick to and invade tissues and avoid the immune system.
These proteins contribute to how harmful the bacteria are during skin infections by mediating adhesion, invasion, biofilm formation, and immune evasion.
Clumping factor B (ClfB) is a surface protein that helps S. aureus attach inside the nose by binding to a skin protein called loricrin in the cornified envelope.
Loricrin is part of the outer skin layer inside the nose called the cornified envelope.
Before this study, the role of ClfB in skin and soft tissue infections (SSTI) was unknown.
ClfB is important for forming abscesses and controlling bacterial numbers early in skin infection by binding to loricrin in the infected tissue.
This binding affects how the abscess forms and how many bacteria grow at the start of infection, as loricrin is expressed within the abscess tissue.
A vaccine targeting ClfB triggers antibody and immune cell responses that protect against S. aureus skin infection.
The vaccine reduced abscess size and bacterial levels in infected mice by inducing both humoral and cellular immune responses.
ClfB is a promising antigen for future vaccines against S. aureus skin and soft tissue infections.
Dengue virus (DENV) causes about 100 million symptomatic infections worldwide each year.
DENV is a common mosquito-borne virus affecting many people globally.
DENV infection can range from mild dengue fever (DF) to severe dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF).
DHF is a more dangerous form of dengue that can threaten life.
Severe dengue symptoms usually appear 5 to 7 days after fever starts during the critical phase.
The reasons why some patients worsen from DF to DHF at this time are not well understood.
Researchers used mass spectrometry to analyze blood serum from adult DF and DHF patients at critical and recovery phases.
This method measures many small molecules called metabolites in the blood.
At the critical phase, 29 metabolites differed between DF and DHF patients, including bile acids, purines, acylcarnitines, phospholipids, and amino acids.
Bile acids were up to five times higher in DHF patients and linked to increased liver injury markers AST and ALT.
AST and ALT are enzymes that indicate liver damage when elevated.
Uric acid, a key antioxidant in blood, was 1.5 times lower in DHF patients than in DF patients.
Lower uric acid may reduce the body's defense against harmful oxidative stress.
During recovery, eight metabolites including the bile acid chenodeoxyglycocholic acid remained altered in DHF patients.
This suggests that liver effects from severe dengue may last beyond the critical phase.
The study identified altered metabolic pathways linked to DHF during critical and recovery phases.
These metabolic changes improve understanding of DHF and point to possible new treatment targets.
The levels of substrate receptor proteins in Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) are tightly controlled to keep all CRL types functional and avoid trapping core components.
Substrate receptors help CRLs recognize targets, so their balance is essential.
Misregulation of substrate receptor parts of CRLs, especially SCF ligases, is linked to diseases including cancer.
F-box proteins, the substrate receptors of SCF ligases, are normally controlled by tagging themselves for destruction within intact SCF complexes.
This tagging leads to their breakdown by the cell's protein recycling system called the proteasome.
When Met30 is not bound to Skp1, due to mutations or cadmium stress, it is rapidly degraded by the cell.
Met30 is a yeast F-box protein that normally binds Skp1 as part of SCF ligases.
A new degradation pathway targets Met30 that is free from Skp1 and requires the cullin protein Cdc53/Cul1 but not Skp1.
This shows that Cdc53 can act independently of Skp1 in degrading Met30.
The SCF core proteins Cdc53, Rbx1, and the enzyme Cdc34 work together to tag unbound Met30 for degradation without Skp1.
This tagging process is called ubiquitylation and marks Met30 for destruction.
Cdc53 and Rbx1 can directly bind Met30 without Skp1, attaching at a region near the F-box domain.
This binding depends on a specific sequence called the degron region that controls Met30 stability.
This Skp1-independent degradation pathway is important for chromosome stability and helps yeast survive heavy metal stress like cadmium.
Cadmium stress causes Met30 to detach from Skp1, increasing the need for this alternative degradation route.
Many decisions arise from the accumulation of noisy evidence until it reaches a threshold.
This process is known as the bounded evidence accumulation model.
This mechanism explains how stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence.
Stimulus strength is often measured by the signal-to-noise ratio of the information.
The model paradoxically predicts that an increase in noise leads to higher confidence.
Higher noise also leads to faster decisions because evidence reaches the boundary more quickly.
Researchers used random dot motion to add unbiased noise to the visual cortex.
The researchers verified this sensory manipulation using neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST.
In both humans and monkeys, increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence.
These effects occurred over a range of stimuli where accuracy was minimally impaired.
The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of the model.
This indicates a common mechanism explains how volatility influences choices across different species.
Increased volatility makes the accumulated evidence reach the decision boundary more rapidly.
This rapid movement explains why noisy evidence can result in faster choice times.
The manipulation added a second level of randomness to the visual display.
This method increased volatility without changing the average strength of the motion signal.
High volatility increased the confidence of the monkeys despite a negligible effect on accuracy.
Monkeys indicated confidence by choosing between a guaranteed small reward or a larger reward.
The Shigella flexneri effector protein OspI suppresses the human inflammatory response by deamidating the enzyme UBC13 at position Q100.
Shigella flexneri is a pathogen that causes severe diarrhea by invading the intestine and hiding from the immune system.
Deamidation of UBC13 inhibits the synthesis of K63-linked polyubiquitin chains, which prevents the activation of the NF-κB immune signaling pathway.
Normally, UBC13 and TRAF6 must bind to trigger chemical signals that call for immune cells to clear the infection.
Deamidation of the protein UBC13 inhibits its interaction with the protein TRAF6RING.
The bacterial modification specifically targets the binding interface where the two proteins usually meet.
The deamidation of UBC13 at Q100 creates a new intramolecular salt-bridge that competes with a critical intermolecular salt-bridge at the UBC13/TRAF6 interface.
A salt-bridge is an electrical attraction between a positive and negative part of a protein.
Electrostatic repulsion between the negatively charged glutamate (E100) and the TRAF6 RING surface prevents necessary transient interactions.
Because both the modified site on UBC13 and the surface of TRAF6 are now negatively charged, they push each other away.
The bacterial effector OspI from Shigella flexneri inhibits host immune responses by modifying transient protein-protein associations and using salt-bridge competition.
This study shows how a tiny chemical change can have a massive effect on how proteins find and stick to each other during an infection.
Working memory depends on the coordinated interaction of distributed brain networks.
Working memory is the ability to hold and manipulate information in the mind over short periods.
Brain regions may exchange information by synchronizing their rhythmic electrical activity.
These rhythmic waves occur when many brain cells send signals at the same time.
Researchers used transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to manipulate brain waves in healthy volunteers.
The researchers applied 6 Hz stimulation to the right frontoparietal network of the brain.
The frontoparietal network involves regions at the front and side of the brain that support memory.
Stimulation targeted the middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule.
Synchronous stimulation improved reaction times during difficult memory tasks.
This improvement occurred during the 2-back task but not the easier 1-back task.
Participants had to monitor number sequences and spot repeated patterns.
Brain scans showed that synchronous stimulation increased activity in the parietal region.
Increased activity in the right inferior parietal lobe led to faster responses.
The parietal lobe is a part of the brain involved in processing sensory information and spatial reasoning.
The timing of the electrical stimulation changed how different parts of the network communicated.
This stimulation increased functional connectivity between the parietal and frontal areas.
Functional connectivity measures how well different brain areas work together.
The study provides evidence that synchronization across large networks drives cognitive performance.
The results show a direct link between brain synchronization and working memory performance.
The granular retrosplenial cortex is essential for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
These behaviors include navigation, learning, and memory.
Researchers used optogenetic mapping in mice to study the granular retrosplenial cortex.
This region contains low-rheobase neurons and regular-spiking neurons.
The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum provide spatial information to low-rheobase neurons.
Low-rheobase neurons are specialized to receive compass-like signals about where an animal is facing.
Regular-spiking cells process non-spatial information from the claustrum and anterior cingulate.
Regular-spiking cells handle data from different brain regions while their neighbors handle space.
Parallel processing is enabled by precise anatomical organization within layer 1.
The physical layout of the brain wiring ensures that the two types of information do not get mixed up.
Low-rheobase neurons can compute the speed of head rotation.
Low-rheobase cells calculate how fast the mouse is turning even when incoming signals only say which way the mouse is facing.
Low-rheobase neurons are the primary subtype for encoding spatial information.
This discovery identifies a specific cell type that is likely responsible for the ability to stay oriented in space.
The granular retrosplenial cortex is critical for knowing where a person is and how to get to a destination.
Damage to the retrosplenial cortex causes spatial disorientation similar to symptoms seen in Alzheimer’s disease.
Precise axonal and dendritic arborization within layer 1 permits this parallel processing.
Stable flower shapes are important for reproductive success and attracting pollinators.
Petals are usually required to open the flower and help attract pollinators.
Petal number is invariant in Arabidopsis thaliana flowers.
These flowers consistently produce four petals.
Cardamine hirsuta exhibits variable petal numbers ranging from zero to four.
This species can display a variable number of petals on a single plant.
Divergence in the floral regulator APETALA1 accounts for the difference in petal number robustness.
This gene is also known as AP1.
Arabidopsis thaliana AP1 confers robustness by masking the effects of quantitative trait loci.
These quantitative trait loci are also called QTL.
The Cardamine hirsuta version of the AP1 gene fails to complement this function.
Differences in regulatory regions contribute to this divergence.
Variable petal number is maintained in Cardamine hirsuta despite standing genetic variation.
Natural populations have enough variation to produce four-petalled flowers.
The AP1 gene in Arabidopsis thaliana hides the expression of other genetic traits.
This masking ensures the plant consistently grows four petals.
The divergence mapped to upstream regulatory rather than coding regions.
The Cardamine hirsuta AP1 gene does not provide the same stability.
Arabidopsis thaliana is a common research model that maintains flower shape despite genetic differences.
Invariant floral forms are robust to natural perturbations.
The AP1 gene acts like a buffer to hide genetic variations.
Masking prevents other genes from changing the petal count.
Researchers used laser-capture microdissection to isolate and profile genes in the Schmidtea mediterranea intestine.
Schmidtea mediterranea is a flatworm that can regenerate its entire digestive system after injury.
The study identified over 1,800 intestine-enriched transcripts using this sensitive bulk tissue method.
This approach found 809 transcripts that previous single-cell studies did not detect because laser-capture microdissection allows researchers to focus on specific bulk tissue sections.
The planarian intestine performs consolidated roles that humans split among several different organs.
These roles include functions typically handled by the human liver and small intestine, such as energy storage and nutrient absorption.
The study found regionalization of gene activity between the medial and lateral intestinal domains.
This spatial specialization is particularly evident in cells called goblet cells, which are organized into distinct zones within the digestive tract.
The gene gli-1 is required for goblet cells to undergo regeneration after injury.
A second gene called RREB2 is needed for the maintenance of these cells, acting as a transcription factor that turns other genes on or off.
This genetic atlas provides a resource for investigating how the digestive system repairs itself.
These findings support comparative analyses to understand human gastrointestinal pathologies by generating new insights into cellular processes that are often dysregulated in disease.
Understanding how simple animals like planarians regrow their gut could eventually help treat human conditions like acid reflux or surgical damage.
Mitochondria require mechanisms to recognize and remove misfolded proteins to maintain essential functions.
Mitochondria are essential to cellular bioenergetics and metabolism.
Quality control pathways for misfolded mitochondrial proteins are currently poorly defined.
A universal Mitochondria-Associated Degradation pathway for mitochondrial outer membrane proteins has not been described.
Researchers established temperature-sensitive mitochondrial outer membrane proteins as model substrates in yeast.
The researchers used the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae for these experiments.
The model proteins are degraded from the mitochondrial outer membrane by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
The proteins remain on the mitochondria when the proteasome is not working.
Ubiquitination of the substrates is mediated by the ubiquitin ligases Ubr1 and San1.
San1 and Ubr1 normally handle misfolded proteins in the cytosol and nucleus.
Mitochondria-associated degradation of misfolded proteins requires the SSA family of Hsp70 chaperones.
The Hsp40 chaperone Sis1 is also required for this process.
Degradation involves the Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 AAA-ATPase complex and the transmembrane adaptor Ubx2.
Ubx2 has a discrete and functional pool located at the mitochondria.
The study identifies a unique quality control pathway using both cytosolic and mitochondrial factors.
This pathway is distinct from endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation.
The SSA1 chaperone is specifically required for the ubiquitination step of these mitochondrial substrates.
Sis1 slowed the turnover of both model proteins used in the study.
Ubiquitinated mitochondrial quality control substrates require the Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex for efficient proteasomal degradation.
The protein Doa1 is also implicated in the degradation of these substrates.
MicroRNAs are small molecules that regulate how genes are expressed in cells.
The specific molecule miR-9 is highly abundant within the brain.
The role of miR-9 in dendritic and synaptic development was previously unknown.
Dendrites are the branched structures that neurons use to receive signals.
Researchers developed a transgenic miRNA sponge mouse to inactivate the miR-9 family.
The miRNA sponge acts as a trap that binds and sequesters the molecules.
The study found that miR-9 controls dendritic growth and synaptic transmission in vivo.
Synaptic transmission is the process where neurons communicate at specialized junctions.
The downregulation of the transcriptional repressor REST is essential for dendritic growth.
By reducing REST levels, miR-9 allows genes for growth to remain active.
Inhibition of miR-9 results in aberrant dendritic growth in living organisms.
This abnormal growth is accompanied by an impairment in synaptic transmission.
A key function of miR-9 is to keep REST levels low during maturation.
REST is a protein that normally functions to silence specific gene elements.
The transgenic mouse line allows for inactivation in a spatio-temporal-controlled manner.
This method allows scientists to study miR-9 at specific times and locations.
MicroRNAs function as posttranscriptional regulators of gene expression.
These conserved noncoding RNAs are found across many different species.
The protein REST is also known as the RE-1 silencing transcription factor. miR-9 binds to and interferes with the RNA molecules needed to make REST.
Ross River virus is a significant mosquito-borne pathogen in Australia and the Pacific Islands.
Researchers built a mechanistic model to understand how temperature drives this virus.
This virus infects 2,000 to 9,000 people each year and can cause long-term joint pain.
Because mosquitoes cannot control their body temperature, their ability to spread diseases depends on the temperature of their environment.
Transmission of the Ross River virus peaks at a moderate temperature of 26.4°C.
This specific middle temperature allows the virus to spread most effectively.
The relationship between temperature and transmission is not a straight line.
There is a specific middle temperature where the virus spreads most effectively.
Ross River virus transmission stops at thermal limits of 17.0°C and 31.5°C.
The disease cannot spread if the environment is too cold or too hot.
Biological traits of the mosquitoes and the virus prevent the disease from spreading at these extremes.
The virus is endemic year-round in tropics but seasonal in temperate areas.
Low temperatures in temperate regions force transmission to zero for part of the year.
In the tropics, temperatures stay within the transmission range all year.
Cooler areas experience winter temperatures that drop below the virus limit.
Climate warming will increase transmission in temperate areas but decrease it in tropical areas.
Warming may push tropical temperatures above the upper thermal limit for the virus.
Tropical areas are already near the ideal temperature.
Further warming will make them too hot for the virus.
Warming in cooler areas will bring them closer to the ideal range.
Nonlinear models are essential for predicting disease responses to climate change.
These models account for specific temperature limits rather than assuming a simple increase.
Traditional models might assume that more heat always means more disease.
This study shows that the hump-shaped response to temperature is critical for accurate planning.
The specific behavioral correlates of motor cortical beta oscillations remain unresolved in neuroscience.
Beta oscillations are brain waves that emerge when individuals are paying attention or waiting.
Researchers recorded motor cortex activity while three macaques performed a novel neurofeedback task.
The researchers used electrodes to monitor brain activity as the monkeys learned tasks.
The monkeys volitionally brought their beta oscillatory power to an instructed state before reaching.
The monkeys controlled a cursor on a screen using only their brain activity.
Trials with high beta power resulted in slower movement onset times during arm reaches.
Reaches preceded by a reduction in beta power exhibited significantly faster movement onset times.
Population neural activity shifts farther from a movement onset state during beta oscillations.
High beta power moves the neural state further from the threshold required for movement.
This study establishes a neural basis for slowed movement onset following beta oscillatory activity.
The generation of beta oscillations favors a state that compromises readiness for upcoming movements.
Motor cortical beta oscillations have been reported for decades without a clear behavioral function.
Understanding these oscillations might reveal how they contribute to symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.
The monkeys were trained to perform a sequential beta neurofeedback arm-reaching task.
This method allowed researchers to link population neural activity to specific behaviors.
Distances to the movement onset threshold are greatest when the brain reaches a high beta target.
The brain's collective neural activity moves into a state that is mathematically distant from the state needed to trigger a movement.
The brain uses these waves to pause the motor system which makes it harder to start moving quickly.
Beta oscillations favor a low-risk state that ensures the animal remains still.
Some viruses like Marburg and Dengue activate and benefit from the Nrf2 protein to help them infect cells.
Nrf2 is a protein that normally helps cells turn on anti-oxidant genes to protect themselves.
Sulforaphane is a natural compound found in cruciferous vegetables that can activate the Nrf2 protein.
Sulforaphane is produced in cruciferous vegetables after they are damaged or chewed.
Sulforaphane treatment stops HIV from infecting macrophages but it does not work in T cells.
Macrophages and T cells are both types of white blood cells that HIV targets.
When Nrf2 levels are lowered, HIV infects macrophages more easily and Sulforaphane becomes less effective.
Researchers used a technique called siRNA to specifically reduce the amount of Nrf2 in the cells.
The ability of Sulforaphane to fight HIV depends on its ability to activate and move the Nrf2 protein.
This confirms that the drug works by triggering the cell's own internal defense system.
Sulforaphane blocks infection after entry but before formation of 2-LTR circles.
2-LTR circles are markers that show the virus has reached the cell nucleus.
This anti-viral effect does not use the common defense proteins SAMHD1 or MX2 that usually stop HIV.
This suggests Nrf2 uses a previously unknown pathway to block the virus.
This discovery shows that HIV can be blocked by Nrf2 activation in a novel way.
This provides a potential new strategy for HIV treatment by triggering the body's own antioxidant response.
Aedes-borne arboviruses like dengue and Zika cause increasing morbidity and mortality worldwide.
Arboviruses are viruses transmitted to humans by mosquitoes such as Aedes mosquitoes.
A Zika outbreak in the Dominican Republic allowed researchers to compare transmission drivers.
This outbreak followed a large dengue epidemic in the same region.
About 75% of dengue cases occurred in people aged <20 years.
Zika infections were more widely dispersed across different age groups in the population.
Reported Zika infections were highly clustered among females at 73.8% of cases.
This percentage shows a significant difference in reported cases between men and women.
Guillain-Barre syndrome attack rates were slightly higher in males than in females.
Guillain-Barre syndrome is a serious neurological condition sometimes triggered by the Zika virus.
Existing dengue immunity had little impact on the reported attack rates of Zika.
Prior exposure to dengue did not seem to change the risk of Zika infection.
Awareness campaigns likely drove increased health seeking behaviour among women of reproductive age.
This behaviour explains why more Zika cases were reported in women than in men.
Media campaigns and screening are recommended for women of reproductive age during outbreaks.
These strategies help identify cases in groups at higher risk for specific complications.
Anabaena filaments develop nitrogen-fixing heterocysts separated by about ten vegetative cells during nitrogen deprivation.
Anabaena is a multicellular cyanobacterium that grows in long chains called filaments.
Researchers used a hetR-gfp fusion to track fluctuations of the essential transcription factor HetR.
HetR is a master regulator protein that controls how cells change into heterocysts.
Fluctuations in hetR expression in nearby cells are coupled across two to three cells.
This coupling sets the spatial scale for how individual cells interact along the filament.
These correlations arise primarily from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Cells communicate by passing molecules through channels instead of just inheriting traits during division.
Fluctuations after nitrogen deprivation build up on those present under nitrogen-replete conditions.
Random variations in gene activity exist even when nitrogen is plentiful for the cells.
The inhibitor PatS, communication via SepJ, and HetR auto-regulation determine these expression fluctuations.
PatS acts as a brake while HetR reinforces its own production through auto-regulation.
The study highlights differences between inhibitors PatS and HetN and septal proteins SepJ and FraC/FraD.
Different proteins manage communication and inhibition depending on the level of nitrogen availability.
Stochasticity and communication combine to control the one-dimensional developmental pattern in Anabaena.
The organism manages random genetic noise to ensure heterocysts are spaced correctly along the filament.
Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings through a process known as dual-adaptation.
Visuomotor mapping refers to how the brain coordinates visual information with physical body movements.
Participants performed a target-pointing task where researchers manipulated the offset of visual feedback.
The researchers prevented participants from seeing their own arm during the pointing task.
Target shapes morphed between spiky and circular forms served as a continuous contextual cue.
These shapes signaled which specific movement adjustment the participant needed to make.
A Bayesian learning model called a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters describes this associative learning process.
This model predicts that the brain uses categorisation rather than extracting a linear rule.
Participants apply the mapping for the trained shape most similar to the current cue.
Using these shape cues to guide movement requires explicit awareness of their role.
The learning rate decreases systematically as the number of training pairs increases.
Learning slows down when participants must manage more shape-mapping associations at once.
The Bayesian model provides a possible mechanism for learning multiple visuomotor mappings simultaneously.
This suggests the brain manages complex tasks by grouping similar experiences together.
Many countries lack the baseline data necessary to plan and launch public health programs for neglected tropical diseases.
Neglected tropical diseases cause significant physical debilitation and lowered economic productivity, but programs cannot start without data.
Researchers developed the Integrated Threshold Mapping methodology to simultaneously map four specific neglected tropical diseases.
The protocol targets lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM protocol determines if a disease has reached the threshold for intervention rather than providing exact prevalence figures.
A country must prove a disease has passed a specific threshold established by the World Health Organization before starting treatment.
The study compared the Integrated Threshold Mapping methodology with standard WHO methodologies in one district each in Mali and Senegal.
Researchers compared both methodologies in terms of feasibility, cost, time, and human resource needs.
The ITM methodology reached the same conclusions as standard WHO methods for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The new methodology resulted in more targeted intervention recommendations for schistosomiasis by using the sub-district as the measurement unit.
The ITM methodology was found to be practical, feasible, and more cost-effective than standard mapping methods.
The methodology resulted in a 31% cost saving in Mali and a 19% saving in Senegal by using resources more efficiently.
The Integrated Threshold Mapping tool could help endemic countries implement necessary public health programs more easily.
This first activity can help with further collaboration for implementing integrated public health interventions.
Organ aging is associated with reduced stem cell occupancy in the niche.
The niche is a specialized environment that houses and supports stem cells.
Notch signaling increases with age in Drosophila female germline stem cells.
This increased signaling results in the removal of stem cells from the niche.
Notch signaling regulates the adhesion of germline stem cells to the niche.
The pathway alters adhesion by changing the expression of the protein E-cadherin.
The age-dependent increase of Notch signaling is partially mediated by Sex lethal.
A reduction in the protein Sex lethal helps drive this signaling change.
BMP signaling levels remain unaffected in stem cells with defective Notch signaling.
BMP signaling is a separate pathway that promotes the self-renewal of stem cells.
Notch signaling in the niche cells decreases as the organism ages.
This reduction in the niche contrasts with the increase seen in stem cells.
These findings regarding Notch and adhesion may be relevant to metastatic cancer.
In metastatic cancer cells, Notch signaling is also known to suppress cell adhesion.
Notch signaling in the niche cells is necessary to maintain niche integrity.
The reduction of signaling in these cells helps explain how aging disrupts the stem cell environment.
Elimination of Sex lethal in germline stem cells elevates Notch signaling.
This elevation of signaling triggers early loss of the stem cells from their environment.
HIV infection currently cannot be cured but can be controlled using combinations of multiple anti-retroviral drugs.
These anti-retroviral drugs work together to keep the virus at low levels in the body.
Because HIV genotypes vary between individual patients, it is difficult to determine which drug combination will provide effective treatment.
Each patient carries a unique version of the virus that may respond differently to specific medications.
Existing HIV treatment models are typically based only on viral sequence data and do not account for the chemical similarity of drugs.
These models ignore how the physical structure of a drug affects its ability to stop the virus.
Researchers applied proteochemometric models that combine chemical properties and protein target properties into a single bioactivity model.
This method analyzes both the genetic makeup of the virus and the chemistry of the drugs simultaneously.
Proteochemometric models performed better than models based only on sequence data in resistance classification.
The new approach more accurately predicted how much a virus would resist a specific drug treatment.
The study identified previously unpublished mutations in HIV Reverse Transcriptase and HIV Protease that confer drug resistance.
These specific genetic changes allow the virus to survive even when exposed to standard anti-viral medications.
The proteochemometric models achieved an 84% correct resistance prediction rate when applied to the public Stanford University HIV resistance database.
This high success rate demonstrates the model's ability to handle real-world data from a large patient population.
The researchers added an applicability domain to the prediction tool to inform users about the reliability of specific predictions.
Staphylococcus aureus expresses cell wall-anchored proteins to invade host tissues and achieve immune evasion.
These specialized proteins allow the bacteria to stick to host cells while hiding from defenses.
The protein clumping factor B, or ClfB, facilitates Staphylococcus aureus nasal colonization.
ClfB helps the bacteria live in the nose by interacting with the cornified envelope.
Researchers discovered that ClfB is a virulence determinant during Staphylococcus aureus skin infection.
This finding shows the protein is a key factor in how the bacteria cause disease.
ClfB promotes the development of a skin abscess by binding to the host ligand loricrin.
Loricrin is a specific protein found in human skin that the bacteria latch onto.
ClfB influences the abscess structure and bacterial burden within the first 12 hours of infection.
The protein is crucial for determining how the infection organizes early in the process.
A model vaccine targeting ClfB induces protective humoral and cellular immune responses.
This vaccine triggers both antibodies and immune cells to defend against the skin infection.
ClfB is an important candidate antigen for future SSTI vaccines.
Targeting this antigen could help prevent difficult-to-treat skin and soft tissue infections.
Dengue virus causes approximately 100 million symptomatic infections every year.
Dengue is a viral infection spread by mosquitoes that affects millions of people globally.
Dengue infection ranges from mild dengue fever to life-threatening dengue hemorrhagic fever.
Dengue fever is abbreviated as DF and dengue hemorrhagic fever as DHF.
Researchers used mass spectrometry-based metabolomic profiling to analyze the blood sera of patients.
Metabolomic profiling is the study of small molecules in the blood called metabolites.

Working memory depends on the coordinated interaction of distributed brain networks.

Stimulation targeted the middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule.

Participants had to monitor number sequences and spot repeated patterns.

The granular retrosplenial cortex is essential for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.

Low-rheobase neurons are specialized to receive compass-like signals about where an animal is facing.
Regular-spiking cells process non-spatial information from the claustrum and anterior cingulate.
Regular-spiking cells handle data from different brain regions while their neighbors handle space.
Parallel processing is enabled by precise anatomical organization within layer 1.
The physical layout of the brain wiring ensures that the two types of information do not get mixed up.
Low-rheobase neurons can compute the speed of head rotation.
Low-rheobase cells calculate how fast the mouse is turning even when incoming signals only say which way the mouse is facing.
Low-rheobase neurons are the primary subtype for encoding spatial information.
This discovery identifies a specific cell type that is likely responsible for the ability to stay oriented in space.

Precise axonal and dendritic arborization within layer 1 permits this parallel processing.
Stable flower shapes are important for reproductive success and attracting pollinators.

MicroRNAs are small molecules that regulate how genes are expressed in cells.

This method allows scientists to study miR-9 at specific times and locations.

Ross River virus is a significant mosquito-borne pathogen in Australia and the Pacific Islands.

There is a specific middle temperature where the virus spreads most effectively.

Low temperatures in temperate regions force transmission to zero for part of the year.

Cooler areas experience winter temperatures that drop below the virus limit.

Further warming will make them too hot for the virus.
Warming in cooler areas will bring them closer to the ideal range.

The specific behavioral correlates of motor cortical beta oscillations remain unresolved in neuroscience.
Beta oscillations are brain waves that emerge when individuals are paying attention or waiting.

The researchers used electrodes to monitor brain activity as the monkeys learned tasks.

Reaches preceded by a reduction in beta power exhibited significantly faster movement onset times.
Population neural activity shifts farther from a movement onset state during beta oscillations.
High beta power moves the neural state further from the threshold required for movement.

The generation of beta oscillations favors a state that compromises readiness for upcoming movements.

This method allowed researchers to link population neural activity to specific behaviors.
Distances to the movement onset threshold are greatest when the brain reaches a high beta target.
The brain's collective neural activity moves into a state that is mathematically distant from the state needed to trigger a movement.
The brain uses these waves to pause the motor system which makes it harder to start moving quickly.
Beta oscillations favor a low-risk state that ensures the animal remains still.
Some viruses like Marburg and Dengue activate and benefit from the Nrf2 protein to help them infect cells.
Nrf2 is a protein that normally helps cells turn on anti-oxidant genes to protect themselves.
Sulforaphane is a natural compound found in cruciferous vegetables that can activate the Nrf2 protein.
Sulforaphane is produced in cruciferous vegetables after they are damaged or chewed.

Macrophages and T cells are both types of white blood cells that HIV targets.

Researchers used a technique called siRNA to specifically reduce the amount of Nrf2 in the cells.
The ability of Sulforaphane to fight HIV depends on its ability to activate and move the Nrf2 protein.
This confirms that the drug works by triggering the cell's own internal defense system.

2-LTR circles are markers that show the virus has reached the cell nucleus.
This anti-viral effect does not use the common defense proteins SAMHD1 or MX2 that usually stop HIV.
This suggests Nrf2 uses a previously unknown pathway to block the virus.
This discovery shows that HIV can be blocked by Nrf2 activation in a novel way.
This provides a potential new strategy for HIV treatment by triggering the body's own antioxidant response.

Arboviruses are viruses transmitted to humans by mosquitoes such as Aedes mosquitoes.
A Zika outbreak in the Dominican Republic allowed researchers to compare transmission drivers.
This outbreak followed a large dengue epidemic in the same region.
About 75% of dengue cases occurred in people aged <20 years.
Zika infections were more widely dispersed across different age groups in the population.

This percentage shows a significant difference in reported cases between men and women.

These shapes signaled which specific movement adjustment the participant needed to make.

The protocol targets lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM protocol determines if a disease has reached the threshold for intervention rather than providing exact prevalence figures.
A country must prove a disease has passed a specific threshold established by the World Health Organization before starting treatment.
The study compared the Integrated Threshold Mapping methodology with standard WHO methodologies in one district each in Mali and Senegal.
Researchers compared both methodologies in terms of feasibility, cost, time, and human resource needs.
The ITM methodology reached the same conclusions as standard WHO methods for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The new methodology resulted in more targeted intervention recommendations for schistosomiasis by using the sub-district as the measurement unit.

Organ aging is associated with reduced stem cell occupancy in the niche.

The pathway alters adhesion by changing the expression of the protein E-cadherin.

A reduction in the protein Sex lethal helps drive this signaling change.
BMP signaling levels remain unaffected in stem cells with defective Notch signaling.
BMP signaling is a separate pathway that promotes the self-renewal of stem cells.

This reduction in the niche contrasts with the increase seen in stem cells.

The reduction of signaling in these cells helps explain how aging disrupts the stem cell environment.

This elevation of signaling triggers early loss of the stem cells from their environment.

Targeting this antigen could help prevent difficult-to-treat skin and soft tissue infections.

The deamidase OspI from Shigella flexneri changes glutamine 100 in UBC13 to glutamate.
This modification is called Q100E deamidation.

Working memory is supported by coordinated interactions among large-scale brain networks, especially frontal and parietal regions.
Oscillatory synchronization in the theta frequency range helps coordinate neuronal activity across distant brain regions during working memory.
Theta frequency means brain waves oscillating between 4 and 8 Hz.
Causal evidence for how oscillatory activity shapes brain networks and behavior in humans is limited, so tACS was used to modulate brain oscillations.
Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) applies weak electrical currents to influence brain rhythms.
Theta-frequency (6 Hz) tACS was applied to the right middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule to modulate frontoparietal network synchronization during working memory tasks.
Synchronous tACS means stimulation at 0° relative phase; desynchronous means 180° relative phase.
Synchronous tACS improved working memory performance during high cognitive demand tasks like the 2-back test.
The 2-back task requires remembering items presented two steps earlier, making it more difficult than 1-back.

The effects of tACS on brain activity depend on the relative phase of stimulation and the cognitive state during the task, as shown by simultaneous fMRI. fMRI measures brain activity without interference from electrical stimulation artifacts.
Synchronous tACS during verbal working memory tasks increased parietal brain activity, which correlated with better behavioral performance.
The parietal cortex is a brain region involved in maintaining information during working memory.
The relative phase of frontoparietal tACS influences functional connectivity and information flow within the working memory network.
Synchronous stimulation increased frontal connectivity, while desynchronous increased posterior connectivity.
Working memory performance is directly linked to large-scale brain synchronization across a right frontoparietal network.
The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
The RSG helps process information about location and other types of behavior, but how it does this is not well understood.
Optogenetic circuit mapping in mice was used to study specific circuits in the RSG.
This method activates neurons with light to trace connections from different brain regions to the RSG.
The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum selectively recruit low-rheobase (LR) pyramidal cells in the superficial RSG.
These brain areas provide spatial information that targets LR neurons in the RSG.

Motor cortical beta oscillations have been reported for decades but their behavioral correlates remain unresolved.
Beta oscillations are rhythmic brain activity in motor areas linked to movement control.
The study recorded neural activity from motor cortex of three macaque monkeys performing a novel neurofeedback task.
The neurofeedback task involved monkeys controlling their brain waves before making arm reaches.

Monkeys controlled a cursor by increasing or decreasing beta oscillations and held it steady to trigger reaching.
Reaches preceded by reduced beta power had significantly faster movement onset times than those preceded by increased beta power.
Higher beta power was linked to slower start of arm movements across all three monkeys.
Population neural activity shifted farther from the movement onset state during beta oscillations.
This shift occurred for both neurofeedback-induced and naturally occurring beta oscillations during reaching tasks.
The study establishes a population neural basis for slowed movement onset following beta oscillatory activity.
Beta oscillations mark brain states linked to delayed initiation of new movements.
Marburg virus, KSHV, and Dengue virus activate and benefit from Nrf2, but HIV infection is blocked by Nrf2 activation.

Macrophages and T cells are different types of immune cells targeted by HIV.

2-LTR circles are DNA forms made before HIV integrates into the host genome.

Activating Nrf2 can strongly block HIV infection and reveals a new antiviral mechanism.
Aedes-borne arboviruses such as dengue and Zika continue to cause epidemics worldwide.

Zika infections were significantly more common among females, who made up 73.8% of cases and had age-adjusted attack rates of 7.64 per 10,000 versus 2.72 per 10,000 in males.

R0 measures the average number of new infections caused by one infected person.

Under nitrogen deprivation, Anabaena filaments develop a one-dimensional pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts separated by about ten photosynthetic vegetative cells.

This coupling defines the scale of cellular interactions along the filament.
Correlations in hetR expression between cells mainly arise from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Molecules passing between cells coordinate gene activity more than inheritance from cell division.

Linked fluctuations form a base pattern before nitrogen removal and intensify during early development.

These factors shape gene activity even when development is not triggered.

PatS acts earlier, while HetN and FraC/FraD affect later stages and specific molecular transport.

Activation, inhibition, and cell-cell communication proteins combine with stochastic gene expression to control coupled fluctuations that generate the one-dimensional developmental pattern in Anabaena filaments.
Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings when feedback for each mapping is provided alternately.
This process is called dual-adaptation.
Learned context cues allow switching between stored visuomotor mappings.
Context cues are signals that help select the correct movement pattern.
Little is known about how associative learning between contextual cues and visuomotor mappings generalises to novel but similar conditions.
Generalisation means applying learned movements to new but related targets.
Participants performed a rapid target-pointing task with visual feedback offsets that depended on target shape.
Different shapes required different hand movements to hit the targets.
Target shapes formed a continuous set morphed between spiky and circular shapes.
The shape provided a continuous cue for which visuomotor mapping to use.
After training, participants were tested without feedback on novel target shapes not seen before.
This tested whether learning generalized to new shapes.
The study compared explicit linear generalisation with an implicit Bayesian learning model predicting categorisation.
The Bayesian model predicts using the mapping of the closest trained shape.
Learning the associations requires explicit awareness, and participants generalise by applying the mapping of the trained shape most similar to the current one.
Participants unaware of the shape-mapping link did not learn to adjust their movements.
The Bayesian learning model predicts learning slows down with more training pairs, which was confirmed experimentally.
Learning many shape-movement pairs at once causes interference and slows learning.
The Bayesian learning model offers a mechanism for simultaneously learning multiple visuomotor mappings.
This model uses a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters to track each shape-mapping pair separately.
Vertical control and elimination programs focused on neglected tropical diseases can reduce infection prevalence and intensity.
Many NTD-endemic countries lack baseline data needed to start or expand control programs.
An integrated mapping approach for overlapping NTDs could save resources and improve efficiency.

The diseases included lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.

It assesses whether an area has reached levels that require health actions.
The ITM protocol uses WHO-recommended disease indicators and age groups with adapted sampling for field use.
For schistosomiasis, sampling was done at the sub-district level instead of ecological zones.
The ITM protocol was tested against WHO mapping methods in one district each in Mali and Senegal.
The ITM method agreed with WHO methods on interventions for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
For schistosomiasis, ITM gave more targeted intervention recommendations at the sub-district level.
The ITM method was practical, feasible, and showed overall cost savings compared to WHO methods.
ITM used fewer vehicles, smaller teams, and less time in the field in Mali and Senegal.
This integrated mapping tool could help implement needed NTD programs in endemic countries.
Stem cells naturally stay in a special environment called the niche, which is designed to support them.
As organs age, fewer stem cells remain in their niche, but the reasons are not well understood.
Notch signaling increases with age in Drosophila female germline stem cells, causing their removal from the niche.
Stem cells with low Notch signaling stick better to the niche by increasing E-cadherin, out-competing neighbors with higher Notch levels.
E-cadherin is a molecule that helps cells attach to each other and to their environment.
Increasing Notch signaling in stem cells speeds up their age-related loss from the niche, partly controlled by the gene Sex lethal.
Blocking Notch signaling in stem cells does not delay their loss with age or affect BMP signaling that supports stem cell renewal.
BMP signaling is a pathway that helps stem cells renew themselves.
Notch activity decreases with age in niche cells, weakening niche integrity and affecting stem cell retention.
Niche cells support stem cells and help keep them attached.
Notch signaling controls stem cell adhesion to the niche during aging and also reduces adhesion in metastatic cancer cells.
HIV infection cannot currently be cured but can be controlled by combination treatment with multiple anti-retroviral drugs.
Different viral genotypes occur in virtually every patient, so the best drug combination must be chosen for effective treatment.
Computational models using viral genotypic and clinical phenotypic data can predict optimal treatment regimens for individual HIV patients.
Current models for HIV drug resistance prediction use only viral sequence data and ignore chemical similarity of drugs.
Proteochemometric models combine chemical and protein target properties in a single bioactivity model to improve resistance prediction.
Proteochemometric modeling integrates drug chemistry with viral mutations to better capture drug-target interactions.
The study used a large clinical database with about 300,000 drug-mutant bioactivity data points across multiple drug classes and thousands of HIV mutants.
Proteochemometric models achieved a prediction error below 0.5 Log Fold Change and outperformed previous sequence-only models in resistance classification.
The models confirmed known and identified previously unpublished resistance-conferring mutations in HIV Reverse Transcriptase and HIV Protease.
Applying the models to the public Stanford HIV resistance database resulted in an 84% correct resistance prediction rate, better than previous work.
Proteochemometric models can accurately predict phenotypic resistance from genotypic data even for novel HIV mutants and mixtures.
An applicability domain was added to inform users about prediction reliability based on sequence similarity and training data density.
This measure helps indicate when model predictions are more or less trustworthy.
Staphylococcus aureus expresses cell wall-anchored proteins that mediate adhesion, invasion, and immune evasion, contributing to its virulence.

Loricrin is a protein in the skin's outer layer that ClfB binds to during nasal colonization.
The role of ClfB during skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI) had not been previously investigated.
This study reveals a novel role for ClfB during Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections.

Loricrin is present in the abscess wall and allows ClfB to help bacteria form abscesses and grow early in infection.
Vaccination targeting ClfB induces protective humoral and cellular immune responses and protects against Staphylococcus aureus skin infection.
The vaccine triggers antibodies and T cells that reduce abscess size and bacterial burden in infected skin.
ClfB is identified as an important antigen for future vaccines against Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections.
Dengue virus (DENV) causes about 100 million symptomatic dengue infections each year.
DENV infection can cause mild dengue fever (DF) or severe dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF).
The critical phase occurs 5–7 days after fever starts when DHF symptoms usually appear.
The reasons why some patients progress from DF to DHF are not well understood.
Researchers used mass spectrometry to profile metabolites in blood from adult DF and DHF patients at critical and recovery phases.
Twenty-nine metabolites differed between DF and DHF patients at the critical phase, including bile acids, purines, acylcarnitines, phospholipids, and amino acids.
Bile acids were up to fivefold higher in DHF patients than in DF patients and correlated with elevated liver enzymes AST and ALT.
Higher bile acid levels indicate liver injury in DHF patients.
Uric acid was 1.5 fold lower in DHF patients compared to DF patients, indicating reduced antioxidant defense and increased oxidative stress.
Uric acid is the most abundant antioxidant in blood.
At recovery, eight metabolites including the bile acid chenodeoxyglycocholic acid remained altered in DHF patients.
This shows prolonged liver impact after severe dengue infection.
Altered metabolic pathways linked to DHF were identified in both critical and recovery phases.
These changes provide insights into host-virus interactions and DHF disease mechanisms.
Some altered metabolic pathways in DHF may serve as potential therapeutic targets.
The abundance of substrate receptor subunits of Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) is tightly controlled to maintain the full set of CRLs.
Substrate receptor subunits help CRLs recognize specific target proteins.
Misregulation of substrate receptor components of CRLs, especially SCF ligases, has been linked to diseases including cancer.
F-box proteins, the substrate receptors of SCF ligases, are regulated by autocatalytic ubiquitylation followed by proteasome-mediated degradation.
Autocatalytic ubiquitylation means F-box proteins tag themselves for destruction by the cell's protein recycling system.
A separate degradation pathway acts on the yeast F-box protein Met30 when it is dissociated from Skp1.
This pathway targets Met30 that is not bound to its usual partner Skp1.
This non-canonical degradation pathway requires the cullin component Cdc53/Cul1 but is independent of Skp1.
Cdc53/Cul1 is part of the SCF core, while Skp1 is usually essential but not needed here.
The pathway involves SCF core components Cdc53, Rbx1, and the ubiquitin conjugating enzyme Cdc34 but does not require Skp1.
Cdc34 attaches ubiquitin to Met30, marking it for degradation without Skp1 involvement.
This Skp1-independent degradation pathway is critical for chromosome stability and defense against heavy metal stress in yeast.
Heavy metal stress causes Met30 to dissociate from Skp1, triggering this degradation pathway.
Many decisions arise by accumulating noisy evidence until a threshold or bound is reached.
This process is described by a bounded accumulation model that tracks evidence over time.
The brain makes decisions by gathering uncertain information over time until enough evidence supports one.
In perception, stimulus strength measured by signal-to-noise ratio affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence.
Stronger signals lead to faster, more accurate decisions with higher confidence.
Stronger sensory signals (higher signal-to-noise) lead to faster, more accurate decisions and higher confidence.
An increase in noise causes faster decisions, reduced accuracy, and paradoxically higher confidence in bounded evidence accumulation.
Higher noise speeds the decision variable toward the bound, shortening reaction time and raising confidence when evidence is weak.
Adding noise makes decisions quicker and less accurate, but surprisingly, people feel more confident about.
The study used a sensory manipulation that added unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex.
This manipulation was confirmed by neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT and MST.
Increasing noise caused faster decisions and greater confidence in humans and monkeys with minimal loss of accuracy.
The effect was strongest at low motion strengths where accuracy was only slightly impaired.
The size of noise effects on decision speed and confidence matched predictions of the bounded evidence accumulation model.
This model links motion strength and volatility to choice, reaction time, and confidence through a common mechanism.

Researchers implanted electrodes in monkeys' motor cortex and trained them to change their beta brain.
Monkeys volitionally modulated their motor cortical beta oscillatory power before executing arm reaches.
Monkeys controlled a cursor by increasing or decreasing beta oscillations and held it steady to trigger reaching.
Monkeys controlled a cursor on a screen by changing their beta brain waves, holding it.
Reaches preceded by reduced beta power had significantly faster movement onset times than those preceded by increased beta power.
Higher beta power was linked to slower start of arm movements across all three monkeys.
Population neural activity shifted farther from the movement onset state during beta oscillations.
This shift occurred for both neurofeedback-induced and naturally occurring beta oscillations during reaching tasks.
The study establishes a population neural basis for slowed movement onset following beta oscillatory activity.
Beta oscillations mark brain states linked to delayed initiation of new movements.
Marburg virus, KSHV, and Dengue virus activate and benefit from Nrf2, but HIV infection is blocked by Nrf2 activation.
While several viruses use Nrf2 to help their infection, HIV is uniquely blocked when Nrf2 is activated.
The effect of Nrf2 activation on HIV infection had not been tested before this study.
Sulforaphane (SFN) from cruciferous vegetables activates Nrf2 to strongly change gene expression.
SFN is a powerful mobilizer of Nrf2, a master regulator of the antioxidant response.
SFN blocks HIV infection in primary macrophages but not in primary T cells.
Macrophages and T cells are different types of immune cells targeted by HIV.
Lowering Nrf2 levels in macrophages increases HIV infection and reduces SFN's antiviral effect.
SFN blocks HIV after viral entry but before 2-LTR circle formation, like the antiviral proteins SAMHD1 and MX2.
2-LTR circles are DNA forms made before HIV integrates into the host genome.
SFN does not increase levels of the antiviral proteins SAMHD1 or MX2 during HIV inhibition.
Activating Nrf2 can strongly block HIV infection and reveals a new antiviral mechanism.
Aedes-borne arboviruses such as dengue and Zika continue to cause epidemics worldwide.
The Dominican Republic had a large dengue epidemic followed closely by Zika virus cases, allowing study of their different transmission drivers.
Retrospective surveillance data were used to analyze national outbreaks of dengue, Zika, and Guillain-Barre syndrome in the Dominican Republic.
Dengue cases were mostly in people under 20 years old, while Zika infections were spread more evenly across age groups.
Dengue attack rates were slightly higher in males at 25.9 per 10,000 compared to 21.5 per 10,000 in females.
Zika infections were significantly more common among females, who made up 73.8% of cases and had age-adjusted attack rates of 7.64 per 10,000 versus 2.72 per 10,000 in males.
The basic reproduction number (R0) for Zika was higher in females at 1.84 than in males at 1.72.
R0 measures the average number of new infections caused by one infected person.
Guillain-Barre syndrome attack rates were slightly higher in males at 0.62 per 10,000 than in females at 0.57 per 10,000 during the Zika outbreak.
Guillain-Barre syndrome is a nerve condition linked to Zika infection.
Existing dengue immunity had little impact on Zika attack rates at the population level.
Community awareness campaigns likely increased reporting of Zika infections among women of reproductive age, though biological susceptibility cannot be ruled out.
Media campaigns and screening are recommended for women of reproductive age during Zika outbreaks.
Under nitrogen deprivation, Anabaena filaments develop a one-dimensional pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts separated by about ten photosynthetic vegetative cells.
The transcription factor HetR, essential for heterocyst differentiation, was studied using a chromosomal hetR-gfp fusion under nitrogen-rich and nitrogen-poor conditions.
The chromosomal fusion allowed precise measurement of HetR gene expression fluctuations.
Expression fluctuations of hetR in nearby cells along Anabaena filaments are coupled with a spatial range of about two to three cells.
This coupling defines the scale of cellular interactions along the filament.
Correlations in hetR expression between cells mainly arise from intercellular molecular transfer rather than cell division.
Molecules passing between cells coordinate gene activity more than inheritance from cell division.
Fluctuations in HetR expression exist under nitrogen-rich conditions and build up after nitrogen deprivation, showing continuity in gene expression dynamics during development.
Linked fluctuations form a base pattern before nitrogen removal and intensify during early development.
Basal expression of the HetR inhibitor PatS, cell-cell communication via SepJ, and positive HetR auto-regulation determine hetR expression fluctuations under nitrogen-rich conditions.
These factors shape gene activity even when development is not triggered.
The HetR inhibitors PatS and HetN differ in their roles during development, and septal proteins SepJ and FraC/FraD differ in their effects on hetR expression and cell communication.
PatS acts earlier, while HetN and FraC/FraD affect later stages and specific molecular transport.

Activation, inhibition, and cell-cell communication proteins combine with stochastic gene expression to control coupled fluctuations that generate the one-dimensional developmental pattern in Anabaena filaments.
Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings when feedback for each mapping is provided alternately.
This process is called dual-adaptation.
Learned context cues allow switching between stored visuomotor mappings.
Context cues are signals that help select the correct movement pattern.
Little is known about how associative learning between contextual cues and visuomotor mappings generalises to novel but similar conditions.
Generalisation means applying learned movements to new but related targets.
Participants performed a rapid target-pointing task with visual feedback offsets that depended on target shape.
Different shapes required different hand movements to hit the targets.
Target shapes formed a continuous set morphed between spiky and circular shapes.
The shape provided a continuous cue for which visuomotor mapping to use.
After training, participants were tested without feedback on novel target shapes not seen before.
This tested whether learning generalized to new shapes.
The study compared explicit linear generalisation with an implicit Bayesian learning model predicting categorisation.
The Bayesian model predicts using the mapping of the closest trained shape.
Learning the associations requires explicit awareness, and participants generalise by applying the mapping of the trained shape most similar to the current one.
Participants unaware of the shape-mapping link did not learn to adjust their movements.
The Bayesian learning model predicts learning slows down with more training pairs, which was confirmed experimentally.
Learning many shape-movement pairs at once causes interference and slows learning.
The Bayesian learning model offers a mechanism for simultaneously learning multiple visuomotor mappings.
This model uses a Mixture-of-Kalman-Filters to track each shape-mapping pair separately.
Vertical control and elimination programs focused on neglected tropical diseases can reduce infection prevalence and intensity.
Many NTD-endemic countries lack baseline data needed to start or expand control programs.
An integrated mapping approach for overlapping NTDs could save resources and improve efficiency.
Researchers developed and tested an integrated mapping protocol called Integrated Threshold Mapping for four NTDs.
The diseases included lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM protocol is resource-efficient and determines if disease thresholds for public health interventions are met.
It assesses whether an area has reached levels that require health actions.
The ITM protocol uses WHO-recommended disease indicators and age groups with adapted sampling for field use.
For schistosomiasis, sampling was done at the sub-district level instead of ecological zones.
The ITM protocol was tested against WHO mapping methods in one district each in Mali and Senegal.
The ITM method agreed with WHO methods on interventions for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
For schistosomiasis, ITM gave more targeted intervention recommendations at the sub-district level.
The ITM method was practical, feasible, and showed overall cost savings compared to WHO methods.
ITM used fewer vehicles, smaller teams, and less time in the field in Mali and Senegal.
This integrated mapping tool could help implement needed NTD programs in endemic countries.
Stem cells naturally stay in a special environment called the niche, which is designed to support them.
As organs age, fewer stem cells remain in their niche, but the reasons are not well understood.
Notch signaling increases with age in Drosophila female germline stem cells, causing their removal from the niche.
Stem cells with low Notch signaling stick better to the niche by increasing E-cadherin, out-competing neighbors with higher Notch levels.
E-cadherin is a molecule that helps cells attach to each other and to their environment.
Increasing Notch signaling in stem cells speeds up their age-related loss from the niche, partly controlled by the gene Sex lethal.
Blocking Notch signaling in stem cells does not delay their loss with age or affect BMP signaling that supports stem cell renewal.
BMP signaling is a pathway that helps stem cells renew themselves.
Notch activity decreases with age in niche cells, weakening niche integrity and affecting stem cell retention.
Niche cells support stem cells and help keep them attached.
Notch signaling controls stem cell adhesion to the niche during aging and also reduces adhesion in metastatic cancer cells.
HIV infection cannot currently be cured but can be controlled by combination treatment with multiple anti-retroviral drugs.
Different viral genotypes occur in virtually every patient, so the best drug combination must be chosen for effective treatment.
Computational models using viral genotypic and clinical phenotypic data can predict optimal treatment regimens for individual HIV patients.
Current models for HIV drug resistance prediction use only viral sequence data and ignore chemical similarity of drugs.
Proteochemometric models combine chemical and protein target properties in a single bioactivity model to improve resistance prediction.
Proteochemometric modeling integrates drug chemistry with viral mutations to better capture drug-target interactions.
The study used a large clinical database with about 300,000 drug-mutant bioactivity data points across multiple drug classes and thousands of HIV mutants.
Proteochemometric models achieved a prediction error below 0.5 Log Fold Change and outperformed previous sequence-only models in resistance classification.
The models confirmed known and identified previously unpublished resistance-conferring mutations in HIV Reverse Transcriptase and HIV Protease.
Applying the models to the public Stanford HIV resistance database resulted in an 84% correct resistance prediction rate, better than previous work.
Proteochemometric models can accurately predict phenotypic resistance from genotypic data even for novel HIV mutants and mixtures.
An applicability domain was added to inform users about prediction reliability based on sequence similarity and training data density.
This measure helps indicate when model predictions are more or less trustworthy.
Staphylococcus aureus expresses cell wall-anchored proteins that mediate adhesion, invasion, and immune evasion, contributing to its virulence.
Clumping factor B (ClfB) helps Staphylococcus aureus stick inside the nose by binding with high affinity to loricrin in the anterior nares.
Loricrin is a protein in the skin's outer layer that ClfB binds to during nasal colonization.
The role of ClfB during skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI) had not been previously investigated.
This study reveals a novel role for ClfB during Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections.
ClfB is crucial for abscess structure and bacterial burden early in skin infection through a specific interaction with loricrin expressed in abscess tissue.
Loricrin is present in the abscess wall and allows ClfB to help bacteria form abscesses and grow early in infection.
Vaccination targeting ClfB induces protective humoral and cellular immune responses and protects against Staphylococcus aureus skin infection.
The vaccine triggers antibodies and T cells that reduce abscess size and bacterial burden in infected skin.
ClfB is identified as an important antigen for future vaccines against Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections.
Dengue virus (DENV) causes about 100 million symptomatic dengue infections each year.
DENV infection can cause mild dengue fever (DF) or severe dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF).
The critical phase occurs 5–7 days after fever starts when DHF symptoms usually appear.
The reasons why some patients progress from DF to DHF are not well understood.
Researchers used mass spectrometry to profile metabolites in blood from adult DF and DHF patients at critical and recovery phases.
Twenty-nine metabolites differed between DF and DHF patients at the critical phase, including bile acids, purines, acylcarnitines, phospholipids, and amino acids.
Bile acids were up to fivefold higher in DHF patients than in DF patients and correlated with elevated liver enzymes AST and ALT.
Higher bile acid levels indicate liver injury in DHF patients.
Uric acid was 1.5 fold lower in DHF patients compared to DF patients, indicating reduced antioxidant defense and increased oxidative stress.
Uric acid is the most abundant antioxidant in blood.
At recovery, eight metabolites including the bile acid chenodeoxyglycocholic acid remained altered in DHF patients.
This shows prolonged liver impact after severe dengue infection.
Altered metabolic pathways linked to DHF were identified in both critical and recovery phases.
These changes provide insights into host-virus interactions and DHF disease mechanisms.
Some altered metabolic pathways in DHF may serve as potential therapeutic targets.
The abundance of substrate receptor subunits of Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) is tightly controlled to maintain the full set of CRLs.
Substrate receptor subunits help CRLs recognize specific target proteins.
Misregulation of substrate receptor components of CRLs, especially SCF ligases, has been linked to diseases including cancer.
F-box proteins, the substrate receptors of SCF ligases, are regulated by autocatalytic ubiquitylation followed by proteasome-mediated degradation.
Autocatalytic ubiquitylation means F-box proteins tag themselves for destruction by the cell's protein recycling system.
A separate degradation pathway acts on the yeast F-box protein Met30 when it is dissociated from Skp1.
This pathway targets Met30 that is not bound to its usual partner Skp1.
This non-canonical degradation pathway requires the cullin component Cdc53/Cul1 but is independent of Skp1.
Cdc53/Cul1 is part of the SCF core, while Skp1 is usually essential but not needed here.
The pathway involves SCF core components Cdc53, Rbx1, and the ubiquitin conjugating enzyme Cdc34 but does not require Skp1.
Cdc34 attaches ubiquitin to Met30, marking it for degradation without Skp1 involvement.
This Skp1-independent degradation pathway is critical for chromosome stability and defense against heavy metal stress in yeast.
Heavy metal stress causes Met30 to dissociate from Skp1, triggering this degradation pathway.
